title: Bills' Bye Week Evaluations: How Have Remade Special Teams Units Fared?
full_text:
Despite offense and defense getting most of the attention, and most of the playing time, there are three phases of football, and the Buffalo Bills are quietly dominating the one that goes the most unmentioned.
Buffalo's special teams units are producing at some of the best rates in the league, turning kicking, punting and returning into a strength for the team to lean on.
Here's how well special teams coordinator Jeff Rodgers' units have been producing through six weeks.
Tyler Bass has missed two extra points this season, but is a perfect 13-for-13 on field goals this season. In fact, he's made 18 straight field goals dating back to 2024, the longest streak by a Bills kicker since Rian Lindell had 18 in 2007.
The Bills haven't called upon Bass to kick in the 50+ yard range, but he is 5-for-5 on kicks between 40 and 49 yards, including a clutch game-winner in overtime against the Rams.
On the flip side, Greg Rousseau won AFC Special Teams Player of the Week for his blocked kick against the Rams, saving the game and allowing Bass the opportunity to drill that 45 yarder. His play marked the first blocked kick in OT that led to a win since 2015.
Joe Andreessen, who recently earned a three-year extension , is currently tied for fifth with nine special teams tackles already this year, on pace to beat his mark of 23 last year which was second in the NFL.
Rookie Tommy Doman Jr. hasn't been called upon much this season. In fact, the Bills have punted just 12 times so far this season, the lowest mark in the NFL. Still, the seventh-rounder has made the most of his limited opportunites.
After two weeks, Doman ranked third in the league in EPA/punt above expected on his four punts. Through six weeks, his 12 punts have traveled 584 yards, while allowing just 32 return yards.
The rookie's 45 net yards per punt is currently the best mark in the NFL, and Buffalo's 32 total return yards on punts is the third best in the league behind only Seattle (11) and Carolina (31).
After being an All-Pro kick returner last year, Ray Davis has picked up where he left off. He currently leads the league in kick return average with 31.0 yards per return, after being the only player last season to average over 30 yards per return. Greg Dortch also ranks 21st with 26.0 yards per return on his 18 attempts.
He hasn't taken one to the house yet, but Davis took the opening kickoff against the Rams 70 yards to start the game, the longest return for the Bills on an opening kickoff since Nyheim Miller-Hines had a 96 yard touchdown return against New England back in 2022.
When Davis returned the opening kickoff against the Raiders 40 yards, he became the first player to return two straight opening kickoffs for 40+ yards since Brad Smith for the Jets in 2010.
After Week 5, the Bills had the sixth-highest special teams EPA at +19.2, according to Ari Meirov .
The phase's performance in Week 6 was praiseworthy from Joe Brady in his press conference on Monday, called the kickoff team "elite" and saying "it's just guys making plays."
Look for Bass, Doman Jr., Davis, Dortch and Andreessen to continue making plays this season that continually put the Bills in positions to succeed in the other two phases of the game.

title: NFL Week 7 Expert Picks Reveal Panthers' Chances to Keep Rolling vs. Buccaneers
full_text:
The Carolina Panthers have won two straight games over playoff hopefuls, and now they return home to face off with a team that's been a thorn in their side: the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
The Bucs may or may not get Baker Mayfield back for this contest, but it will be a heated rivalry game regardless. It will also be crucial for the Buccaneers to cut into Carolina's division lead, so it could be a tough game regardless of how the two teams are perceived right now.
What are the experts saying?
CBS Sports analyst Pete Prisco has not once picked the Panthers to win, and they've proved him wrong thrice. This time, though, he's going with the surging Panthers, although he's still not predicting a big performance.
Prisco picked a one-point Panthers win, saying, "The Bucs might have Baker Mayfield back for this one. That would be big. The Panthers are rolling on offense as Bryce Young is in the MVP conversation. It will stay that way, but the Bucs will hang around."
His CBS colleague John Breech is also picking the Panthers, but he's taking them by a field goal. Arizona Republic's Jeremy Cluff is picking a Panthers win, 24-16, betting on the Bryce Young-led offense to continue clicking at home.
SI's Ian MacMillan isn't buying any of what the Panthers are doing, and he's picking the Buccaneers to upset them in Charlotte.
"Time to sell high on [the Panthers]. Their offense has been phenomenal to start the year, but I have plenty of questions surrounding the ability of some of the defenses they've had to face... I wouldn't be surprised to see them significantly regress. It could start this weekend when they take on a Tampa Bay defense that's fourth in opponent EPA per play and eighth in opponent success rate," he wrote.
Here's how the rest of the SI staff is predicting this one:
Sporting News' Vinnie Iyer disagrees, predicting a 24-17 win. "Jalon Daniels is doing his best to keep the Bucs' competitive with help from the running game. The defense is also bringing a good pass rush of late. Bryce Young is locked in passing all over the field for the Panthers, however and their running game is red-hot with Chuba Hubbard," he wrote.
The Athletic's Nick Kostos picked the Buccaneers straight up and against the spread. If Jalon Daniels starts, he'll take the Panthers, but if it's Mayfield, he believes the Buccaneers will win this one.
"You just get the sense Mayfield will be better when he returns. It’s possible he was pressing after getting his desired contract extension. Mayfield will never be confused with Joe Montana, but he’s a good quarterback," he wrote.
What does this tell us? As mentioned in our coverage of the odds , Baker Mayfield's status is hugely important. But even so, there's a strange amount of belief in the 1-5 Buccaneers and a strange lack of belief in the Panthers.
They can't waltz in expecting to win, in other words.
Zachary Roberts is a journalist with a wide variety of experience covering basketball, golf, entertainment, video games, music, football, baseball, and hockey. He currently covers Charlotte sports teams and has been featured on Sportskeeda, Yardbarker, MSN, and On SI.

title: Panthers' Biggest Need Ahead of the NFL Trade Deadline Is Painfully Obvious
full_text:
With less than three weeks until the NFL trade deadline, the Carolina Panthers can make a move or moves to further bolster their roster as they pursue a second straight NFC South title.
Off to a 3-2 start to the year, Carolina has been one of the league's biggest surprises so far, maybe not because of the record, but because of how they got here.
The offense has been elite, led by QB Bryce Young, who is leading the NFL in passing yards per game, and is the only QB throwing for 300+ per game in the NFL.
Chuba Hubbard has regained his 2024 form , averaging 4.8 yards per carry and posting 6 total touchdowns in five games.
The offensive success is real, and OC Brad Idzik is on fire calling plays in his first season as the playcaller.
All that said, this roster still has holes, areas to clean up, and rooms heavily affected by injury. What better time to improve the roster than at the trade deadline, when teams are willing to sell on talented players.
Over the next three years, Carolina owns all but two of its draft picks and has the Vikings' fourth-round pick in the upcoming draft.
So the Panthers aren't short on draft compensation to make a deal happen, and there's clearly a belief that, given how good the offense is, they can beat top teams in the league. So where would the Panthers look if they made a move at the trade deadline? The answer is obvious.
Both Mike Jackson and Jaycee Horn are out for the foreseeable future. The hope is that the Panthers will get them both back in the latter half of the season, but nothing is guaranteed. Carolina currently ranks 19th in the NFL in pass defense.
Will Lee III has been solid since taking an elevated role, but he still has rookie moments where receivers beat him, most recently last Sunday, when Devonta Smith caught a 19-yard touchdown over him to make it a one-score game.
Carolina will continue to play elite receivers. In just a month, Carolina will face guys like Matthew Golden, Chris Olave, Zay Flowers, and more great pass-catchers. The secondary will need reinforcements.
Our staff has mentioned many corners that make sense for Carolina. It could be a reunion with Chargers corner Donte Jackson, a veteran on the worst team in the NFL who still has good football left in him. A name like Keishon Nixon of the Packers, who is versatile, still 29, and in the last year of his contract, also makes sense.
Those are just two examples of corners who would make sense for Carolina. No matter who the target is, the Panthers have 20 days to get a deal done and keep the secondary afloat while Jackson and Horn recover.
Preston is an experienced sports writer focusing on NFL, College Football, NBA, and MMA topics. He is a passionate Charlotte and Oklahoma sports fan and graduated from the University of Science and Arts Oklahoma in 2025 with a Bachelor of Arts in Communications degree with a focus in journalism.

title: Panthers' Edge Rushers Aren't Making a Huge Impact, But It Doesn't Matter
full_text:
After the 2025 season, there was one area for the Carolina Panthers that had to be the top priority in the offseason. The Panthers were able to win the NFC South and host a playoff game despite having the worst pass rush in the NFL.
Carolina ranked dead last in sacks and in the bottom three in pressure rate, so, naturally, it was the first thing on GM Dan Morgan's list to fix. This, of course, led to the day-one free-agent signing of Jaelan Phillips, who left the Eagles to become the premier pass rusher.
So far in the 2026 season, Carolina ranks 8th in pass-rush win rate, sitting at 54% after Week 6. Along with the pass-rush success, Carolina has allowed the sixth-fewest passing touchdowns this season.
The edge rushers have had their moments this season; Phillip's hasn't been otherworldly but hasn't been a detriment either. That said, he's not the primary reason that Carolina is generating pressure
While Phillips was Carolina's splash signing in free agency, the two best signings so far have been the inside linebacker duo of Devin Lloyd and Bobby Okereke.
Lloyd signed with Carolina early in free agency, and Okereke was added to the roster just 48 hours before the league-wide cut date, and he immediately found his way into the starting lineup.
So far, they've been the defense's highlight. Against the Eagles, Lloyd generated an 82% pass-rush win rate, which is absurd, especially for an inside linebacker. That win rate made history, as ESPN has never recorded a higher one.
From @espn Analytics and @NextGenStats : #Panthers LB Devin Lloyd posted an 82% Pass Rush Win Rate against the #Eagles . According to ESPN Research, that’s the highest by any player in a game since ESPN started tracking win rates in 2017.
This season, Lloyd has posted 2 sacks and 4 quarterback hits, wreaking havoc on opposing QBs. After an All-Pro season in 2025, this is exactly what Carolina signed Lloyd for, and he's exceeded expectations. Lloyd has 0.5 fewer sacks than Jaelan Phillips.
The same can be said for Bobby Okereke, who's especially exceeded expectations, having been signed less than a week before cut day after his release by the New York Giants. According to PFF , Okereke ranks 11th in pass rush grade among qualifying linebackers, posting a 77.5.
Both linebackers have also thrived in pass coverage as well, combining for three interceptions this season, which is huge considering Carolina is down both their starting cornerbacks, Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson.
The defense as a whole is far from perfect , but having versatile veterans in the middle of the field who can contribute against both the run and the pass is crucial to Carolina staying in games and giving the high-powered offense good field position.

title: The Panthers Are Becoming a Different Team When the Pressure Is On
full_text:
Panthers fans have seen enough games go sideways late that you almost expect it. That's why Sunday in Philadelphia caught my attention. The Panthers didn't play a clean game, not even close, but when things got tight late, Carolina played pretty damn well.
The Panthers had 13 penalties for 149 yards, wiped out some big returns and did just about everything possible to keep the Eagles hanging around. Somehow, none of it ended up costing them. And the more I think about it, Philadelphia wasn't the first time we've seen Carolina play some of its best football late in a game.
The Panthers were up 13-7 late in the third quarter when they got the ball backed up at their own 6. This wasn't exactly great field position for a team that had spent most of the afternoon fighting penalties. Then Jalen Coker made one of the biggest plays of the game.
Carolina was facing third-and-9 from its own 10 when Bryce Young found Coker for 32 yards. Chuba Hubbard later broke a 19-yard run on fourth-and-1, and the Panthers eventually went 94 yards on 14 plays. Hubbard finished it off with the touchdown to give Carolina a 19-7 lead.
Philadelphia answered and cut it to 19-14 in the fourth quarter, and Carolina followed that by going three-and-out. Here came the Eagles again with a chance to take the lead, and we've all seen that movie before. This time, the defense got them off the field.
Tre Tyus nearly got to the punt, it went only nine yards and Carolina suddenly had the ball in Philadelphia territory. A few plays later, Young found Tommy Tremble for the touchdown. The Eagles had made their push, but Carolina never let the game get away from it.
That's probably what I liked most about those last few minutes. Everything didn't have to go right. Philadelphia scored, Carolina went three-and-out and the Eagles got the ball back with a chance to take the lead, but the Panthers still found a way to make the plays they needed.
Cleveland is the reason I'm not going to say the Panthers have completely figured this out. Carolina took an 18-13 lead with 4:25 left after Young found John Metchie III for a touchdown. They had a chance to finish that game, too.
Akayleb Evans looked like he had the interception that might have done it, only for Bobby Okereke to get called for roughing the passer. Cleveland got another shot, scored and eventually won 21-18. There were four lead changes in the fourth quarter, and Carolina didn't make enough plays at the end.
That's why I keep coming back to what happened in Philadelphia. Three weeks after letting one get away in Cleveland, the Panthers found themselves in another tight game with an opponent making a late push. This time Carolina was the team making the plays at the end.
Maybe five games isn't enough to say this has become who they are. I'm not going that far yet. But I'm starting to think there's something to it.
Detroit wasn't nearly as close going into the fourth quarter. Carolina was up 29-19, but there was still enough time left for the Lions to make things uncomfortable. Instead, the Panthers took the ball and basically made Detroit stand there and watch.
Carolina went 72 yards on 13 plays, took 5:44 off the clock and got a Ryan Fitzgerald field goal out of it. Nothing spectacular happened, but I loved that drive. You're up 10 in the fourth quarter, so keep the ball, burn almost six minutes and come away with points.
Detroit eventually scored to make it 32-26, but by then there wasn't enough time left for the Lions to get another possession. Carolina had already taken care of that with the drive to start the quarter. Sometimes that's all you need when you're trying to finish a game.
Dave Canales talked Monday about learning how to play with a lead. I don't know if I'm ready to say the Panthers have learned it yet, especially after what happened in Cleveland. But I do think they're getting better at it.
Sunday wasn't just Young making a play or Hubbard taking over. Coker made the third-down catch when Carolina was backed up, Hubbard got the fourth-and-1 and the defense got Philadelphia off the field when the Eagles had a chance to take the lead. Tyus nearly got to the punt, helping Carolina get the short field, and Young finished it with the touchdown to Tremble.
That's a lot of different guys showing up when Carolina needed somebody to make a play. For a long time, it felt like the Panthers needed almost everything to go right to win. One bad penalty, one bad possession or one big play by the other team could change everything.
Sunday definitely wasn't perfect. You don't get 13 penalties for 149 yards and call that a clean afternoon, but Carolina still walked out of Philadelphia with a 25-14 win. Maybe that's another sign this team is starting to figure out how to handle these games.
I'm not trying to turn a 3-2 start into something bigger than it is. Cleveland happened, there are 12 games left and I'm sure there are going to be a few more Sundays that drive all of us crazy. But I'm starting to feel a little different when these games get tight.
Instead of sitting there waiting for something to go wrong, I'm starting to wonder who's going to make the play.
Mark Livingston is a South Carolina native and recent Penn State graduate with a degree in Digital Media and Journalism. He previously wrote for Greenville Sports Media, where he covered various sports and teams across the Carolinas. His experience includes game coverage, feature stories and interviews.

title: Jalen Coker or Tetairoa McMillan? Fantasy Football Owners May Be Asking Wrong Question
full_text:
There was a pretty fair question going into Sunday's game in Philadelphia. What was Jalen Coker's return going to do to Tetairoa McMillan?
McMillan had been putting up some big numbers while Coker was out, including that ridiculous 14-catch, 192-yard game against Detroit. But Coker had been really good when healthy, too. I figured somebody was probably going to lose a few targets once they were finally back on the field together.
Maybe I was worried about the wrong thing.
Coker caught six passes for 97 yards against the Eagles, while McMillan caught six for 86. That's 183 yards between them, and neither one had to disappear for the other to have a good game.
This was the part I was most interested in Sunday. McMillan had become such a big part of the offense while Coker was out, and I didn't want to see Carolina suddenly start taking opportunities away from him just because Coker was back.
That really wasn't an issue. Coker got 13 targets and McMillan got nine, and they were basically on the field the same amount. McMillan played 60 offensive snaps and Coker played 59.
Coker also made one of the biggest catches of the afternoon. Carolina was backed up at its own 10 on third-and-8 when Young found him for 32 yards. Instead of another punt and giving Philadelphia good field position, the Panthers got moving and eventually finished the drive with a Chuba Hubbard touchdown.
McMillan kept getting his chances, too. He caught six passes for 86 yards and has now had at least five catches and 75 yards in four of five games.
That's where having Coker back can actually help McMillan instead of hurting him. Defenses can't spend the whole afternoon worrying about No. 4 when there's another guy on the other side who can go for close to 100 yards.
It's been a while since Carolina has had that.
The Philadelphia game wasn't some completely new development, either. Coker and McMillan both went over 75 yards against Chicago in Week 1, and now they've done it again.
They've only played three games together this season, and they've both gone over 75 in two of them. I'm not ready to say that's going to happen every week, because obviously it isn't, but it's enough to make me think Sunday wasn't some fluke.
And 13 targets for Coker caught my attention. That's a lot for anybody, much less a receiver playing his first game back from an injury. Young clearly wasn't shy about going right back to him.
McMillan still got nine targets of his own, so I'm not sure why we need to be in a hurry to decide which one is Carolina's No. 1 receiver. Maybe that answer becomes obvious as the season goes along, but right now it doesn't really matter.
If they're both getting open, keep throwing it to them.
This is where it gets a little tougher because fantasy owners don't care about everybody being happy. We need to know who we're putting in the lineup.
If you're making me pick one, I'm still taking McMillan. He's been more consistent, and four games with at least 75 yards in five games is enough for me to feel pretty good about putting him out there every week.
But I'm not sitting Coker just because McMillan is playing. Thirteen targets are hard to ignore, especially in his first game back. Coker turned those into six catches for 97 yards, and this was already his second game this season with more than 90 receiving yards.
There are going to be Sundays when one of them gets more work. Maybe McMillan gets 12 targets, and Coker gets seven. Maybe the next week it's the other way around. With two receivers this involved, you're never going to get a perfect 50-50 split.
What Sunday showed me is that I don't think we need one of them to disappear for the other to have a good fantasy day. We've already watched both of them go over 75 yards in the same game twice this season.
That's good for fantasy, but I'm more interested in what it means for Carolina. Young finally has two receivers he looks comfortable throwing to, and if a defense decides it's not going to let McMillan beat it all afternoon, the Panthers have another guy who can make them pay for it.
As for my fantasy lineup, McMillan is staying in it. And if Coker is on my roster, I'm finding a spot for him, too.
Mark Livingston is a South Carolina native and recent Penn State graduate with a degree in Digital Media and Journalism. He previously wrote for Greenville Sports Media, where he covered various sports and teams across the Carolinas. His experience includes game coverage, feature stories and interviews.

title: If Colts Blow It Up, Should Panthers Make a Call About Sauce Gardner?
full_text:
The Panthers are 3-2, coming off a pretty impressive win in Philadelphia, and we're getting to that time of year when trade talk starts picking up. I'm not saying Carolina needs to start throwing draft picks around because it has won three games, but I'm definitely paying more attention when a name like Sauce Gardner comes up.
Evan Sidery pointed out that Indianapolis has several valuable pieces it could move if the Colts eventually decide it's time to reload. Gardner was one of the names he mentioned, along with Jonathan Taylor, Quenton Nelson, DeForest Buckner, Charvarius Ward, and Grover Stewart.
Before we go any further, nobody is reporting that Gardner is available. Nobody is reporting that the Panthers have called about him, either. Indianapolis may have absolutely no interest in trading him, especially after giving up so much to get him less than a year ago.
But the idea got me thinking. If things keep going bad in Indianapolis and the Colts eventually decide they're willing to move some of these guys, would I want Dan Morgan to call about Gardner?
Yeah, I would. The price is where this gets interesting.
We don't need to spend much time explaining why Carolina would want Gardner. He's 25, has already been a first-team All-Pro twice, and is one of the better corners in football. If he ever did become available, there would probably be a pretty long list of teams calling Indianapolis.
I also like that you're not talking about giving up a pick for somebody who might be gone after the season. Gardner signed a four-year, $120.4 million extension, so this would be a move for now and beyond.
Here's the problem. Indianapolis gave up two first-round picks and Adonai Mitchell to get Gardner from the Jets last November. I don't expect the Colts to get all of that back if they ever decided to trade him, but after paying that kind of price, I can't see them being interested in giving him away, either.
That's why I'm calling if I'm Morgan, but I'm also going into the conversation knowing there's a point where I'm out.
I know some people will disagree with me here. Gardner is exactly the kind of player who makes you think about giving up a first-round pick because he's young, proven, and already better than you're hoping most draft picks eventually become.
I'm still keeping the pick.
Carolina is 3-2, and I'm feeling a lot better about this team than I was a few weeks ago. But it's also been five games. I'm not ready to look at the Panthers and say they're one player away from making a serious run, and that's where I'd have a hard time giving up a first-rounder.
A second-round pick is where I'd start getting interested. Maybe Indianapolis wouldn't even consider it. Maybe it would take a second and something else. We really don't know because there's no indication right now that the Colts are trying to trade Gardner in the first place.
There's also his calf injury to check on. Gardner suffered a mild strain Sunday and is considered week-to-week. It doesn't sound like a long-term injury, but if I'm giving up a good draft pick and taking on that contract, I'm making sure everything checks out first.
I probably wouldn't have been interested in this conversation a month ago. If the Panthers had stumbled out of the gate again, I'd be telling Morgan to keep the picks and keep building.
Instead, Carolina is 3-2 and just went into Philadelphia and won 25-14 despite committing 13 penalties for 149 yards. I had plenty to say about those penalties after the game , but the Panthers still found a way to leave with a win.
There are some things happening on offense that have me looking at this team a little differently, too. Bryce Young threw for 281 yards and two touchdowns Sunday. Jalen Coker and Tetairoa McMillan combined for 183 receiving yards, Chuba Hubbard ran for 120, and the defense held Philadelphia to 222 total yards.
There was plenty I liked coming out of the bye , even if there were still a few things that drove me crazy. I'm not ready to call this team a contender yet, but I'm also not against Morgan looking around if there's a move that makes sense.
That's where I am with Gardner. There isn't a trade to make right now because we don't even know if Indianapolis wants to move him. But if that changes and the Colts decide they're willing to listen, I'm calling.
Just don't ask me for that first-round pick.
Mark Livingston is a South Carolina native and recent Penn State graduate with a degree in Digital Media and Journalism. He previously wrote for Greenville Sports Media, where he covered various sports and teams across the Carolinas. His experience includes game coverage, feature stories and interviews.

title: Panthers’ Experienced Linebacker Duo Has Emerged as a Force
full_text:
The Carolina Panthers will host the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Sunday looking for their third straight win. The team returned from its off week this past Sunday and shut down the Jalen Hurts-less Philadelphia Eagles. Dave Canales’s club outgained the Birds, 399-222, in total yards in what proved to be a 25-14 victory.
Six weeks into the season, the Panthers own a 3-2 record and are all alone in first place in the NFC South. The team has won two three straight and three of their last four games following a 59-37 home loss to the Chicago Bears . Quarterback Bryce Young has played exceptional football all season, and Ejiro Evero’s defensive unit has settled in since that forgettable start.
General manager Dan Morgan added several new faces to this side of the ball via free agency in March, and another notable performer after the conclusion of the preseason. Edge rusher Jaelan Phillips (Eagles) inked a four-year, $120 million deal, while 2025 Pro Bowler Devin Lloyd (Jaguars) signed a three-year, $42 million contract.
Finally, Bobby Okereke—late of the New York Giants— joined the club in late August via a one-year, $ 1.5 million deal. It’s the latter two linebackers that have combined to make a huge impact.
DEVIN LLOYD JUST HAD ONE OF THE GREATEST LINEBACKER PERFORMANCES IN NFL HISTORY 9 TKL, 2 TFL, 2 INT, 1 SACK, 1 TD, 1 QBH, 3 PD Carolina may have landed one of the best defensive pickups of the offseason. pic.twitter.com/4BGRbQ7jxq
Lloyd leads Carolina with 35 tackles, despite the fact that he missed the Week 3 game at Cleveland. There’s also a pair of sacks, two interceptions (1 returned for a touchdown), four quarterback hits, and three passes defensed.
Okereke is right behind Lloyd with 34 stops. He’s totaled one sack, a pair of QB hits, one pick, a forced fumble, and four passes defensed. In Sunday’s victory at Philadelphia, he led Carolina with eight stops, three of those for losses, and knocked down two passes.
1st and 10 · Philadelphia Eagles Tanner McKee ( @McKeeTmckee ) is sacked at PHI 15 for an 11-yard loss by Bobby Okereke ( @BobbyOkereke ) https://t.co/p3gaDF1CnO pic.twitter.com/NWlRQomQPK
On the Eagles’ first play from scrimmage, he dropped quarterback Tanner McKee for an 11-yard loss and set the tone for a game in which Nick Sirianni’s team was limited to just 3.6 yards per play.
Best LB duos in the NFL through Week 6: 1. Lloyd/Okereke (CAR) 2. Jones/Thomas (SEA) 3. Edmunds/Reese (NYG) 4. Smith/Simpson (BAL) 5. Oluokun/Miller (JAX) Carolina's LB duo ranked 22nd in these same categories in 2025. Now it's first. Incredible upgrade by Dan Morgan this… pic.twitter.com/mjD8ccCW4W
After six weeks of play, Lloyd is Pro Football Focus’ 14th-ranked linebacker with a 71.8 grade, while Okereke is just two spots below him (70.5).
Again, this has been a much-improved defense still that Week 1 home debacle against Caleb Williams and company. In their last four outings, the Panthers have given up a total of 64 points and surrendered only six offensive touchdowns. That’s a far cry from allowing 552 yards and eight offensive TDs in 60 minutes of play vs. the Bears..
Thanks to these two key offseason additions, as well as contributions from other newcomers, Carolina’s defense appears to finally be making some significant strides.
Russell S. Baxter has been writing and researching the game of football for more than 40 years, and on numerous platforms. That includes television, as he spent more than two decades at ESPN, and was part of shows that garnered five Emmy Awards. He also spent the 2015 NFL season with Thursday Night Football on CBS/NFLN.

title: 3 Panthers Who Came Out of Nowhere in Sunday's Win Over the Eagles
full_text:
There are some pretty easy choices if we're talking about the biggest names from the Panthers' 25-14 win over Philadelphia. Chuba Hubbard ran for 120 yards, Bryce Young threw for 281, and Jalen Coker had 97 yards in his first game back.
But I wanted to go a little deeper than that. There were a few guys who probably weren't getting much attention before the game and ended up having a lot to do with Carolina winning it. One caught two touchdowns, another came up with a huge play on special teams, and the third seemed to be around the ball all afternoon.
Here are three guys I didn't expect to be talking this much about after the game.
Be honest. Who had Tommy Tremble catching two touchdowns Sunday?
Tremble only caught four passes, but he made them count. His first touchdown went for 12 yards and gave Carolina a 10-0 lead in the second quarter. The second one was even bigger because Philadelphia had just cut the lead to 19-14 when Young found him for a 19-yard touchdown.
I liked what Tremble did in the running game, too. Carolina lined him up at fullback on fourth-and-1, and he helped clear the way for Hubbard to break a 19-yard run. The Panthers showed a similar look on another fourth-and-1 later in the drive, and Young got Philadelphia to jump with a hard count.
That's really the thing with Tremble. He can go through a game doing a bunch of little things that most people probably aren't paying attention to, and then you look at the box score, and he has one catch for eight yards. Sunday, he finally got some numbers to go along with all that other stuff.
Four catches, 46 yards and two touchdowns will get your attention.
Tyus is probably my favorite one on this list because you aren't going to understand what he did by just looking at the box score. Philadelphia had cut Carolina's lead to 19-14 in the fourth quarter, and the Eagles were about to get the ball back with a chance to take the lead.
That's when Tyus nearly got to the punt. He deflected it, though it went forward, so it wasn't an official block. The kick went only nine yards, and instead of Philadelphia flipping the field, Carolina got the ball back in Eagles territory. A few plays later, Young hit Tremble for the touchdown that made it 25-14.
Think about how different that looks with a normal punt. Carolina probably starts deep in its own territory, and Philadelphia's defense has a chance to get the ball right back to its offense. Instead, the Panthers were already on the Eagles' side of the field and turned it into seven points.
That's a pretty big moment from a guy most of us probably weren't thinking about when the fourth quarter started.
It didn't take long for Okereke to show up Sunday. On Philadelphia's first offensive play, he came through for an 11-yard sack of Tanner McKee, and he kept popping up from there.
Okereke finished with a team-high 11 tackles, a sack, three tackles for loss, and two passes defended. The Eagles finished with only 222 total yards and 35 on the ground, and Okereke was right in the middle of a lot of what Carolina was doing defensively.
With Devin Lloyd getting so much attention early this season, and deservedly so, I thought Okereke deserved some love after this one. You don't hear his name talked about nearly as much, but Sunday was probably his best game of the season.
From the sack on the first snap to everything he did against the run, this was one of those games where you kept noticing No. 58. Okereke was everywhere, and on a day when Carolina's defense allowed only 222 yards, he was a big reason why.
Mark Livingston is a South Carolina native and recent Penn State graduate with a degree in Digital Media and Journalism. He previously wrote for Greenville Sports Media, where he covered various sports and teams across the Carolinas. His experience includes game coverage, feature stories and interviews.

title: Panthers' Super Bowl Odds Continue to Climb After Impressive Road Win
full_text:
The Carolina Panthers did what they were supposed to do: control the game and find a win on the road against a depleted Philadelphia Eagles team. The 25-14 win moves Carolina to 3-2 on the season and gives them a steady cushion atop the NFC South.
With both the Falcons and Buccaneers losing on Sunday, Carolina's odds of winning the division rose. Winning the division, of course, means making the playoffs, and that means the Super Bowl is in sight.
Does that make Carolina a Super Bowl favorite? Of course not, but the Panthers' Super Bowl odds are rising, and rightfully so.
With wins over the Eagles, Lions, and Falcons, the Panthers are starting to change the national narrative. Theres a consistency, at least on offense, that Carolina hasn't had in the Canales-Young era, but now theres real growth.
As the narrative shifts, so have the current Super Bowl odds. In terms of value, the Panthers could be at a better price than teams that have shorter odds.
Sports Illustrated's Peter Dewey dropped his Week 7 NFL power rankings based on Super Bowl 61 odds . This list isn't based solely on who has the shortest odds, but on which teams offer the best value at their current odds.
With that said, Dewey slotted the Panthers at No. 15. Per DraftKings Sportsbook, the Panthers currently have +5500 odds to win Super Bowl 61, that's the 17th shortest odds in the league.
Meanwhile, the Los Angeles Rams are sitting at +1200 to win the Super Bowl, the sixth-shortest odds, despite being 2-4 on the season and possibly being the NFL's most-injured team.
The Panthers ranked one spot ahead of the Rams in Dewey's power rankings, which is completely justified based soley on value at the current odds.
The Rams are tied for last place in their division. The roster is riddled with injuries to key contributors such as Davante Adams, Myles Garrett, Trent McDuffie, Kobie Turner, and many more.
LA even lost its second kicker of the season after Blake Grupe tore his ACL before his first game with the team concluded.
Meanwhile, the Panthers play in the second-worst division in football, Carolina already has a comfortable lead at the top, and has a division win against the second-best team in the NFC South, the Falcons.
This can easily change if the Rams find a groove and get healthier towards the end of the season, but for right now, it's perfectly fair to like Carolina's Super Bowl odds more than the Rams'.
Preston is an experienced sports writer focusing on NFL, College Football, NBA, and MMA topics. He is a passionate Charlotte and Oklahoma sports fan and graduated from the University of Science and Arts Oklahoma in 2025 with a Bachelor of Arts in Communications degree with a focus in journalism.

title: The Panthers Won in Philadelphia — Here's What I'm Buying and What I'm Not
full_text:
The Panthers went into Philadelphia and came away with a 25-14 win, and there was plenty to like about what they did.
Carolina moved the ball, Bryce Young made some big throws, and the defense never let the Eagles get much going. Jalen Coker also looked pretty comfortable in his first game back, giving Young another weapon alongside Tetairoa McMillan. Still, I'm not ready to get carried away with this one.
Philadelphia was missing some important players and became even more shorthanded as the game went along, so you have to keep that in mind when looking at this win. Carolina deserves credit for taking care of business, but Sunday also gave us a little more to think about with this team.
Let's start here because I don't want it to sound like I'm taking anything away from the Panthers. They went on the road, controlled most of the game, and beat Philadelphia by 11 points. That's a good Sunday, no matter who was on the other side.
But the Eagles weren't close to full strength. Jalen Hurts and Saquon Barkley were already out, and Philadelphia lost more help as the game went along. Carolina wasn't exactly getting the best version of the Eagles.
The Panthers still had to beat the guys who were out there. We've seen Carolina lose enough games over the years that it probably should've won, so I'm not going to hold it against them for taking care of business. The Panthers were the healthier team and played like it.
That's what they were supposed to do.
We've been waiting a few weeks to see what Young would look like with McMillan and Coker on the field together, and Sunday gave us another good look at it. Coker finished with six catches for 97 yards, while McMillan had six for 86. For me, this was probably the most encouraging thing to come out of the game.
That's 183 receiving yards between the two of them, but it's not just about the number. Young had another receiver making plays opposite McMillan, and everything didn't have to go through one guy. Teams are still going to worry about McMillan, but Coker gives them somebody else to deal with.
I'm not expecting those two to combine for nearly 200 yards every week. But Carolina finally got both of them on the field together, and we saw what it could do for Young and the passing game.
Now let's see what it looks like when defenses have a few weeks to adjust to it.
I still don't know how the Panthers managed to have 149 penalty yards and win by 11 points. Carolina was flagged 13 times, and some of them came at the worst possible times. There were several moments where the Panthers would make a play, only to give some of it right back because of a flag.
They got away with it Sunday, but against a healthier team, I'm not so sure they do. That's what's frustrating because Carolina actually did a lot of things well. Young didn't turn the ball over, Chuba Hubbard ran for 120 yards, and the defense held Philadelphia to 222 total yards.
Clean up even some of those penalties, and this game probably isn't as close for as long as it was. Carolina can fix that, but it needs to happen because 149 penalty yards isn't something you're going to keep overcoming.
I don't think Sunday proved the Panthers are suddenly one of the best teams in the NFC, as Philadelphia was too beat up for me to go that far. But I do think we're learning a little more about Carolina. The Panthers are starting to win games they're supposed to win, which hasn't always been a given around here.
Young has more help around him, the defense is doing its part, and Carolina is finding ways to win even when it makes things harder on itself. There's still plenty to fix, and 149 penalty yards is a pretty obvious place to start. But the Panthers went into Philadelphia as the healthier team, handled a game they should've won, and came home 3-2.

title: Bold Predictions For the Chicago Bears Week 7 Matchup Against Patriots
full_text:
The Chicago Bears host the New England Patriots on Thursday night, and both teams will hope to keep their positive momentum after Week 5 victories.
The oddsmakers like Chicago's odds of coming away with a win on their home turf. According to DraftKings Sportsbook , the Bears are currently three-point favorites over the defending AFC Champions.
We finally saw the type of performance we expected from Bears quarterback Caleb Williams and tight end Colston Loveland on Sunday against Atlanta. We like their odds of keeping the good times rolling with the Patriots on deck.
This will be another week where the Bears' offensive success will largely fall on Caleb Williams' shoulders. The Patriots have a stout run defense (allowing 91.8 yards per game on the ground, ninth-best in the league), and Kyle Monangai won't be available for Chicago . D'Andre Swift has also been battling lingering hip and knee injuries in recent weeks and hasn't looked 100%.
Luckily for the Bears, Williams is more than capable of rising to the occasion . He did just that last week against Atlanta, completing 30 of 36 attempts for 306 yards and a touchdown.
With Drake Maye looking much more like the MVP runner-up than the one who struggled in the playoffs (and early this season) in recent weeks, the Patriots will put up more of a fight than Atlanta did. That could cause a slight bump over last week's numbers out of sheer necessity.
We also like Zavion Thomas' odds of having a bigger role this week. Seeing him get three targets over his ten snaps felt like a situation where they want to get his feet wet. With the Patriots focusing on Luther Burden III and Rome Odunze, they'll dial up a deep shot to Thomas, and the rookie's speed will catch them off guard. Williams will benefit with a robust stat line featuring 325 yards and 3 TDs.
Naturally, with Williams going for 325, the Bears pass-catchers will eat. We think Colston Loveland will build upon last week's performance ( when he FINALLY got involved in the passing attack with six grabs for 65 yards and a TD) and eclipse 100 receiving yards against New England.
The Patriots have been strong against tight ends this season with the exception of their Week 5 matchup against Las Vegas. In the other five games, they've allowed an average of 3.8 catches for 31.6 receiving yards to opposing TEs. In that contest, however, Brock Bowers had eight grabs for 110 yards and a receiving TD.
With Loveland's skill set being much closer to Bowers than the other tight ends they've faced, we could see him replicate that performance on Thursday night. He should be a big part of the gameplan each week going forward after a rough start to the season.
The Patriots entered last week's game against the Jets with a precarious offensive line situation, with three players on Injured Reserve (including their starting RG Mike Onwenu). Unfortunately, that situation has become treacherous after three more linemen left the contest with injuries.
Both starting guards have already been ruled out for Thursday night's contest, and tackle Morgan Moses is officially listed as questionable after getting in three limited practices this week. Long story short, their o-line is very banged up, and the Bears should be able to capitalize on that fact .
The Bears are surprisingly tied for fifth in the league with 17 sacks. Their defensive front has vastly outperformed expectations thus far. That trend will continue against New England.
Maye has been sacked only twice over the past three weeks after being taken down three times in each of the Patriots' first three games. Even with the Bears missing a few key defensive linemen, he won't find as much success against Dennis Allen's highly aggressive approach.

title: Mike Vrabel Gives Bears Needed 'TNF' Trench Optimism With Patriots Injury News
full_text:
The Chicago Bears have a battered defensive front, but luckily for Ben Johnson's group, they won't be facing maximum protection against the New England Patriots on Thursday Night Football.
Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel announced that guards Alijah Vera-Tucker and Ben Brown will be absent in Week 7 . In addition, cornerback Carlton Davis III will miss a third straight game with a neck issue.
That's three key players down for New England. The two in the Patriots' interior offensive line are a saving grace for the Bears.
After all, Chicago linebacker Jack Sanborn has been ruled out with a concussion .
Fellow linebacker T.J. Edwards is doubtful with a hamstring issue. Edwards sat out against the Atlanta Falcons this past Sunday.
EDGE Montez Sweat is serving the second game of a suspension for PED use . Sweat will be back after "TNF."
Finally, fellow edge-rusher Dayo Odeyingbo is on the IR with a quad injury .
Vera-Tucker has had a mostly strong year so far after signing with New England this past March, though he did naturally gut through some early-season adjustments with a new group.
The Patriots' starting left guard has excelled in pass-protection in particular, grading out as a 71 by PFF. Overall, Vera-Tucker owns a 68.2 grade, good for the No. 28 ranking league-wide among qualified guards.
In 362 offensive snaps, Vera-Tucker has given up one sack, three quarterback hits, and seven quarterback hurries.
Without him, fellow newcomer Walter Rouse, a sixth-round pick in 2024 to the Minnesota Vikings out of Oklahoma and Stanford, will get the nod.
Rouse had a 65.8 pass-blocking grade with the Vikings during the 2025 season, but was a serious liability in the run game, finishing with a 49.1 grade.
While Vera-Tucker and Brown being out hurts, neither is particularly a world-beater against the run. Against the Bears front, Vrabel wants to establish a strong running game with Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson.
Vrabel was asked about Chicago's vaunted third-down defense, which ranks No. 2 in the NFL through six weeks of the season.
He recognized Dennis Allen's defense's strengths, but insisted on finding a way to impose his offense's will on the ground.
"Yeah, it's excellent. It's very good," Vrabel said of the Bears' defense on third down on Wednesday. "So, I think we have to stay balanced, but also find ways to run the football. They just haven't had a lot of plays against them.
"When you play with the lead, then you don't see a lot of runs. So that's the challenge, is being able to flip the script a little bit, not let them run 73 plays and only have to defend 50."
We'll see if Vrabel can flip the script with backups in the interior offensive line and establish the run. Thus far, the Bears have been the No. 8 run defense during the 2026 season.
Andrew Hughes is a freelance journalist based in Austin, Texas, who has bylines across ON SI and The Sporting News. His work has been featured in The Miami Herald, Bleacher Report, and Yahoo Sports. Andrew graduated from Brooklyn College with a degree in journalism in 2017 and has been a sports fan since 1993.

title: Drawbacks Do Exist for Bears With Safer Caleb Williams Targeting
full_text:
The Bears lead the NFL in time of possession and rushing, and no one can really dislike this.
Still, it's a situation causing at least one disturbing trend.
Bears coaches talk extensively about finding their identity. Look at their stats so far and they seem to be trending toward a more plodding, hold-the-ball team that lacks explosiveness .
In their defense, not having Caleb Williams as quarterback for three of the six starts and a small portion of another game has held them back. However, even in the games he played they had only one game when they showed the real explosiveness anticipated for Year 2 of the Ben Johnson era.
It's not that they're running the ball so much better. They have running it well, except for last week and the game with Green Bay. But some of that can be traced back to the lack of Kyle Monangai as the enforcer type ball carrier who punishes defenses.
Bears are the best team in the NFL when Caleb Williams plays the entire game: 1st in points (45 PPG) 1st in total yards (460/Game) 1st in rushing 1st on 3rd down (61%) 1st in takeaways (3/game) 2nd in sacks And the Bears are #1 in the NFL in time of possession. pic.twitter.com/f3EXcxMy9Q
Last year after six games, the Bears had what they refer to as 17 big plays, or passes of 25 yards or longer. This year, they have seven. In the running game, a big play is 10 yards or longer and they're comparable to last year even without Monangai. They have 24 and last year had 26 at this point.
Explosive plays are a little different than "big plays." Explosive plays are passes of 20 or longer. Getting to the top in this category can be critical and the Bears are nowhere near that point. The Bears are only 14th in explosive play rate at 5.8% according to Sharp Football Analysis.
A few weeks ago, offensive coordinator Press Taylor summed it up fairly well.
"If you're getting explosives, you're probably not eating as much clock," he said. "Where if you're just getting 4 yards here, 6 yards there, 7 yards here, 2 yards here, you're probably going to end up eating a little bit more clock.”
The Bears don't just beat you. They take the ball and don't give it back. Time of possession per game, 2026: 🐻 Bears: 36:01 Vikings: 33:38 Giants: 33:11 #1 in the NFL by more than two minutes a game. The Patriots are 11th at 31:17. Every extra minute Caleb has the ball is a… pic.twitter.com/nSobj30Eov
Buffalo, Baltimore, San Francisco, Kansas City and Green Bay are all teams near the top in explosive play rate and they are to be feared offensively as a result. On Thursday night, the Patriots come in with Drake Maye averaging 8.0 yards per pass attempt. That is a number like a team needs to be a serious Super Bowl threat.
The Bears, meanwhile, average 7.1 per attempt. Williams is at 7.8 so this does make a difference with him at quarterback.
Beyond not having Williams available for half the starts and using weaker-armed backups, there are two possibilities for this drop in explosiveness.
Caleb downfield passing tape. For those of you comparing Caleb to Bo Nix or calling him a checkdown merchant, this is the difference. pic.twitter.com/m82L6e83jW
One is they have drilled the deep targeting out of their quarterback. All Williams has heard since camp started is not to be afraid of the other options on a play or of the checkdown pass.
Williams' average intended air yards so far is 5.8. It's a fraction ahead of Bo Nix for lowest in the NFL. His average air yards per completion is 4.4. That's longer than only Cam Ward, Aaron Rodgers, Baker Mayfield and Nix, among starters. And Mayfield has been injured.
Obviously they are looking shorter and throwing shorter.
Top 5 Fastest QB Runs of 2025 1) Caleb Williams: 21.01 mph 2) Caleb Williams: 20.45 3) Bo Nix: 20.33 4) Caleb Williams: 20.31 5) Caleb Williams: 20.29 pic.twitter.com/GdPq2Al4nB
This isn't necessarily bad if they are piling up the yards after catch. But their top YAC wide receiver is Luther Burden at 20th in the league with 5.2 per catch per NFL Next Gen Stats. Pro Football Reference does have them sixth in YAC as a team at 773 yards but their volume for plays is so high that they will naturally rank higher. They're getting more chances at it.
The other reason for fewer big plays might be how they are limiting themselves by plan.
When the season started, they had this big emphasis on running more 13-personnel packages. That's three tight ends. The Rams did it effectively last year and it became the rage.
The Bears have increased this with rookie Sam Roush as the third tight end with Cole Kmet and Colston Loveland They line up this way with 18% of their plays. Last year it was 8.3%, according to Sharp.
Lowest avg depth of target this season (min 100 dropbacks) Caleb Williams        5.9 Bo Nix                         6.3 Jalon Daniels           6.5 Kyler Murray             7.0 Patrick Mahomes   7.0 Cam Ward                 7.2 pic.twitter.com/TRnlGZfhcv
Using three tight ends can be good for running the ball or getting needed short completions. It's usually not going to increase any team's explosiveness. If you want bigger plays, use faster pass catchers. Wide receivers and running backs are faster. Tight ends are faster, lighter version of linemen.
The Bears are using more than twice as much 13-personnel and it's not necessarily going to up their yards per pass attempt or explosiveness. It can help with ball control.
It's a tradeoff. They're looking shorter keeping the ball longer and churning out first downs but they've had problems in the red zone scoring and aren't getting the big plays they had last year.
At some point, they'll run into a defense again doing the same thing Minnesota did. They blitzed at every opportunity and dared the Bears to beat them deeper.
Caleb Williams is ELITE and goes to his first read less than any QB in the NFL - #Bears https://t.co/cUwHtI6gcx
The problem with pulling back and going ball control too much is when that challenge comes, the offense is ill-equipped to handle the pressure.
It seems almost hypocritical to say after so much criticism went Caleb Williams' way for being too focused on the big passing plays and not enough on the shorter gains, but at some point the Bears will need to challenge downfield or eventually get too bogged down.
Time of possession is fine, and the Eagles used it in 2024 to go on and win the Super Bowl. Normally the top TOP team is somewhere in the playoffs, but not necessarily the winner.
Too much of anything isn't a good thing. It's better balance the Bears need to achieve. A team capable of this can handle anything any opponent throws at them,

title: Kyle Monangai, Jonah Jackson & More Bears Injury Updates From Final Week 7 Practice Report
full_text:
The Chicago Bears have put out their final injury report ahead of the Week 7 game against the New England Patriots and it had both good and bad news for key players.
The three key players we've had our eyes on this week are Kyle Monangai, Jonah Jackson and T.J. Edwards, all of whom are dealing with injuries and were uncertain to play .
Well, the final injury report provided a positive update on one of those players, but negative updates on two of the others.
Here's everything we know from the final injury report of the week before the Bears take on the Patriots on Thursday night.
Monangai is indeed going to sit out another game, and Edwards like will as well with his doubtful tag. Meanwhile, there's a surprise, as Jackson is off the injury report and good to go for Thursday.
That's surprising because a report from ESPN's Jeremy Fowler on Monday said Jackson's status was in doubt due to a hip flexor.
On top of that, we figured Jackson was a long shot given the fact that the Bears are operating on a short week.
Well, we're happy to say we were wrong.
Along with Edwards and Monangai, Jack Sanborn has been ruled out. That will open the door for more snaps for D'Marco Jackson and Noah Sewell, and we might see Keyshaun Elliott get the first defensive snaps of his career.
We have our sights set on a Week 8 return for Monangai, and for good reason.
Johnson has said on more than one occasions that Monangai will not be placed on injured reserve , which signals the Bears don't expect him to miss more than three games.
With his absence for Week 7 on Thursday night now set in stone, Monangai will have missed three contests.
Adding to the optimism for next week, the Bears rusher is going to have 10 more days to get right thanks to the mini bye between now and Week 8, when the Bears will meet the Super Bowl champions, the Seattle Seahawks.
The Bears have had a clear approach to replacing Monangai the last two weeks and we would expect that to continue this week.
That approach has featured Roschon Johnson taking the snaps behind D'Andre Swift, and Zavier Scott being called up from the practice squad to serve as the RB3.
Johnson struggled mightily in Week 5, but, his fourth-quarter fumble notwithstanding, he played far better in Week 6.
He better hold on to the football this week, though, or else he'll find himself in the dog house like Swift was in a few weeks back .
Despite not having Monangai, the Bears haven't leaned more on Swift like we expected. He saw just one second-half carry in the loss to the Green Bay Packers in Week 5 and then only four in Week 6 against the Atlanta Falcons.
Offensive coordinator Press Taylor said the goal there is to try and keep Swift fresh for the long haul of the season, so don't expect to see much of an uptick in his work, barring Johnson landing in the aforementioned dog house with another fumble.
Mike Moraitis is a freelance writer who has covered the NFL for major outlets such as Sports Illustrated and The Sporting News. He has previously written for USA TODAY Sports Media Group and FanSided, and got his start in sports media at Bleacher Report.

title: What Short Week Means for Caleb Williams and Bears in NFL's Ugly Showcase
full_text:
The wild card in Thursday night's matchup for the Bears against the New England Patriots is, of course, just that. It's Thursday night.
They both just played on Sunday and now they need to quickly adjust to playing a game four days later without all of the rest a week can provide tired players or the extra time needed to tweek offensive and defensive schemes meant to deceive.
It's the main reason Thursday Night Football has been known for poor overall play since it started, or at least since "the Butt fumble" by Jets and former Bears QB Mark Sanchez.
Bears coach Ben Johnson humbly admits this lack of prep and recovery time is not an ideal situation.
A Thursday Night Football moment we'll never forget. pic.twitter.com/38NMU492xy
“I wish I had the answers for that one," he said. "I always struggle as a coach of wanting to do more and making sure. Really, at the end of the day, these guys, they just need to go out there and play as fast as they possibly can, play confident football.
"For us, it's just a matter of scaling it back, streamlining it to where they can play fast, they can play clean. If we have another high-penalty game like we did last week, that's not going to play in our favor against a good team like this. We just need to play clean football, and that's really the message throughout, and let our play style come out and show itself again.”
Bo Nix’s passing chart from Thursday night might be the most unethical display of QB play I’ve ever seen 💀 pic.twitter.com/df3Evpefu8
So how has Johnson done at "streamlining" for a short week? The Bears have not played on so little rest under Johnson. They did play on a Friday last year in Philadelphia and handled it quite well, with a 24-15 victory that stunned all the Bears skeptics.
They played their wild card win over Green Bay with one less day off after their regular season ended, and they won 31-27 in a wild comeback.
Johnson seemed to have his offense working well on short rest as Detroit's offensive coordinator. The Lions had a Thursday game in 2024 while with Detroit at Soldier Field and the Lions beat the Bears 23-20. They had their Thanksgiving game the next week but had a full week to prepare for that one.
The Patriots could be going into Thursday night against the Bears without their: FB WR2 WR3 LG RG RT RG2 RG3 CB2
They also beat the Packers 34-20 on a Thursday in Green Bay in 2023 but then lost at home that year in the Thanksgiving Day game to the Packers 29-22. Back one more year to when the Lions weren't quite a playoff team yet, they nearly beat Buffalo at home on Thanksgiving in a 28-25 loss.
Wide receiver Rome Odunze called being ready on short notice as much on the players as the coaches, if not moreso.
"I think the main thing is recovery, just getting the bodies right," he said. "Obviously coming off a short week like that, that’s the main point and just sticking with our details. Being able to go out there and have meaningful reps even though we’re not going full speed is a big factor as well. Just getting the body right, staying on the details."
Thursday night football is the worst .. it’s like watching a high school team practice running plays
The Bears just came off Caleb Williams' most accurate passing day, and the one hope is that kind of timing shown in Atlanta after he had three games away can carry over to Soldier Field.
"I mean, obviously with Caleb coming back, a little bit of that rhythm and that chemistry for sure but at the end of the day, there’s not many things that carry over," Odunze added. "We’ve got to go through it every time we step out there on that field.
"The short week, we’re going to have to go back to our details, back to the things that we did well and try to amplify those."
4-2 is 4-2. Get a W at home on Thursday night and use the mini bye to get healthier.
What they do have working on their side is a little more prep time than the road team has, because the Patriots had to leave on Wednesday to be in Chicago for the Thursday night game. Meanwhile, the Bears can and will use a full day to take a look at what they're doing and "streamline."
It's New England's first Thursday game under Mike Vrabel, although they did play a Wednesday night game but that was to open the season. While he coached Tennessee, Vrabel had a 3-4 record in Thursday games.
Chicago Bears won twice on Thursday night... pic.twitter.com/2JufeIZ2jw
Historically speaking, the Bears are not a bad Thursday team. At least, they have been better than on Monday night or Sunday night.
They are 30-26-2 all time on Thursdays, and this includes day and night Thursday games. On Thursday Night Football, they are 7-8, which is still better than they've fared on Monday night (36-44) or Sunday night (18-32).
Home teams win 55.3% of the time on Thursday night, as opposed to 52.9% in other games, according to Fan Duel.
