title: Raiders Game Review: 3 Takeaways From Week 6 Loss
full_text:
Despite losing their third consecutive game, the Las Vegas Raiders have some things to look forward to.
Las Vegas is on the track long-term, but they have some things to iron out in the short term. Head coach Klint Kubiak has kept his program competitive against two of the league's best teams, the Kansas City Chiefs and Buffalo Bills, coming up short in both matchups but showing they can be a handful for anyone.
I spent some time rewatching Week 6's contest against the Bills. Here are some of my key takeaways and notes from a Raiders game where some players improved while others had their worst day.
$81 million center Tyler Linderbaum had a rough game against the Bills, specifically against Deone Walker, as the mighty size, length, and surreal power may have given the league's best center his worst performance in a long time.
Linderbaum was light on his feet at times (not in a good way), lacked balance, leaned into his blocks, and struggled to anchor when facing a bull rush or speed-to-power. He has had better days, and I don’t expect this performance to be repeated.
Left tackle Kolton Miller had a much better game this week after struggling for the last two games. His anchor was stouter and did a better job of resetting his hands and base when the power element came through. Week 1’s exceptional performance seems like a lifetime ago, but there is a pathway to getting back to more consistent football while figuring out how to handle speed-to-power.
I thought the Raiders did a great job against the Bills' secondary. The issue is finding more consistency with the run game , as it is clear Ashton Jeanty isn’t healthy, but there was a lot to like about the passing game from quarterback Kirk Cousins and his pass-catchers, especially when your top tight ends are the team’s leading receivers.
Kubiak did a good job using exit motions to create confusion for some of the Bills' younger defenders, and it led to some explosive plays from guys like Tre Tucker, who made a big YAC play in the first quarter and the switch release that allowed Tucker to attack the boundary in the red area for his first touchdown.
I also liked how he used out-breaking patterns, especially the popular sail route by Brock Bowers going around where he left the defender looking around for where he had made his break.
Michael Mayer was so good at adjusting his routes and creating separation as a receiver. He is always good at making the first man miss and making up yards after the catch. The Raiders were smart to lock him in for the foreseeable future, making him and Bowers the best tight end duo in the last decade or more.
According to SumerSports , the Bills' standout running back rushed for 4.9 yards per carry when facing stacked boxes. Why was that the case? It was a mixture of two things: Joe Brady’s offensive line making great blocks with good sealing and climbs to the second level, or a lack of ample talent in the middle and opposite of Maxx Crosby.
I thought the flow of the linebackers was good in these instances, but time and time again, the Raiders seemed to struggle to penetrate the backfield without defensive tackle Tonka Hemingway, who may not have made much of a difference, while edge rushers Malcolm Koonce and Kwity Paye continue their tough stretch of performances.
Sunday was rookie safety Treydan Stukes best game in a few weeks. He did a better job defending vertical third, using ample closing speed to the ball carrier for stops in the run game, and having the aggression at the catch point to be both effective and dangerous if the receiver didn't have the concentration or grip strength on the ball. Stukes was also reliable in run fits while playing the alley defender.
MIKE linebacker Nakobe Dean was outstanding, showcasing excellent flow to the ball while having great balance as a tackler to chop his feet and drive through the ball carrier with pop and follow-through. Fellow WILL defender Quay Walker has also been great, but Dean is making the case for being the unquestioned best tackler on the Raiders' defense.
Jared Feinberg, a native of western North Carolina, has written about NFL football for nearly a decade. He has contributed to several national outlets and is now part of our On SI team as an NFL team reporter. Jared graduated from UNC Asheville with a bachelor's degree in mass communications and later pursued his master's degree at UNC Charlotte. You can follow Jared Feinberg on Twitter at @JRodNFLDraft

title: One Week 6 Play That Highlighted the Raiders’ Growth
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders lost to the Buffalo Bills on Sunday, their third straight loss. Yet, several positives still stood out. Among those was how different Las Vegas' defense looked from the Week before. Week 6 confirmed the Raiders are not the team that took the field two Sundays ago.
The Raiders' defense only allowed James Cook and the Bills to rush for 101 total yards. This is notable because of Josh Allen's ability to scramble and Las Vegas' struggles against the run. The 101 yards they allowed were well below their season average of over 130 rushing yards allowed per game.
Against the Bills, Las Vegas' defense eliminated big plays overall. Yet, the unit also eliminated big runs. Cook's biggest gain was 13 yards. Las Vegas allowed long runs of 76 yards and 32 yards against the Kansas City Chiefs and the New England Patriots, respectively, in Weeks 4 and 5.
A loss is a loss, but the Raiders have already won more than they have in the past two seasons. They have lost three games to teams with a legitimate shot at playing in this year's Super Bowl. The need for improvement is clear, but far from unexpected. At 3-3, Las Vegas is ahead of schedule.
Nakobe Dean everybody 🗣️ BUFvsLV on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/xUeN6qxZE0
Furthermore, their growth far outweighs the growth they still need. Few plays on Sunday showed their growth, especially on defense, as Nakobe Dean and Quay Walker helped their teammates along the defensive line get aligned properly. Then, perfectly executed the play.
The attention to detail shown by the Raiders' linebackers is something the unit lacked last season. This play alone shows why Las Vegas' front office added Dean and Walker, especially when compared to last season's linebacker corps. Sunday was another loss, but it was also a learning experience .
During the Raiders' three-game losing streak, they have faced three quarterbacks who are nearly as dangerous running the ball as they are passing it. This impacts the defense's ability to stop the run, as it essentially adds another potential rusher the defense has to concern itself with.
Rushing quarterbacks like Patrick Mahomes, Allen, and Drake Maye can quickly turn into rushes that gash defenses and keep them off balance. This is undoubtedly on the minds of players tasked with stopping them. However, Las Vegas has not only played three mobile quarterbacks with big arms.
They have faced mobile quarterbacks with big arms, who all had running backs who are solid in their own right. Kenneth Walker is tough to bring down regardless of who his quarterback is. The Patriots have multiple running backs the Raiders would love to have on their roster right now.
Cook is one of the league's best running backs with or without Allen. Stopping high-caliber running backs and a quarterback who can, in their own individual way, run as well as those running backs while still throwing the ball anywhere on the field is a tough ask for any defense.
That is what the Raiders have faced, and that has been a major factor in their inability to stop the run this season. That is also what made their run-stopping efforts on Sunday notable, as it showed the unit's return to basics . This Raiders defense is as good as advertised when they are focused.
More specifically, Las Vegas' defense is built to stop the run more than it is built to stop the pass. However, the unit is also borderline elite at rushing the passer,  which requires a different approach than stopping the run. This is part of the chess match coordinators have weekly.
Las Vegas has lost three games in a row, but at least they didn't follow up a terrible game against the   Patriots with another terrible game, as recent Raiders teams would have. That in itself is progress and growth for a team entering its seventh game together.
One of the Raiders' biggest goals entering the season was to show marked improvement under a new coaching staff, with a revamped but not fully rebuilt roster . Even after three consecutive losses, they are well on their way to accomplishing that goal. The Raiders just need to stick to the plan.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: What Raiders Learned About AFC West in Week 6
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders dropped their third consecutive game after falling to the Buffalo Bills 33-30 in Week 6.
While we learned a lot about the Raiders , the Silver and Black gained invaluable knowledge about the rest of its division rivals. Here's what Las Vegas learned about the rest of the AFC West in Week 6.
It wasn't the best performance of the season. However, the Chiefs still coasted by the Los Angeles Chargers 22-6. That being said, Walker III rushed for 128 yards and two touchdowns on 19 carries. The 5-foot-9, 211-pound running back has completely transformed Kansas City's offense, proving to be the most impactful free agency signing of the offseason.
Again, the Chiefs' offense wasn't the best it's been this season, but their floor is exponentially higher with Walker III in the backfield . Through five games, the Super Bowl LX MVP has 665 rushing yards and six rushing touchdowns.
Denver defeated the Seattle Seahawks 17-14 last Thursday, improving its record to 4-2. However, the Broncos won in spite of quarterback Bo Nix. The third-year signal caller completed 17-of-27 passes for 107 yards, averaging four yards per attempt. This isn't a one-off situation for the 26-year-old quarterback. In five of six games, Nix has averaged 5.5 yards or fewer on pass attempts.
The Broncos have a Super Bowl-caliber roster, highlighted by one of the best defenses. Despite that, they don't feel like a true contender because of subpar play from Nix, who is completing 60.3 percent of his passes while attempting 5.6 yards per pass. If Nix's ineptitude continues and the Broncos either miss or flame out in the playoffs, head coach Sean Payton could aggressively pursue another option in the draft or free agency.
As mentioned, the Chargers fell to the Chiefs, plummeting their record to 0-6. Mike McDaniel's joining the staff as the offensive coordinator was supposed to elevate the offense's operation . Instead, the Chargers' offense is one of the worst units in the league, averaging 15.0 points per game (30th), 190.2 passing yards per game (27th), and having a 34.1 third-down conversion rate (27th).
Jim Harbaugh has fielded several questions about potential changes on the coaching staff. The veteran head coach has said that everything is on the table. Regardless of what changes occur in the coming weeks, Los Angeles is already staring down a lost season.
Logan Lazarczyk is a graduate of the University of Missouri-Kansas City, where he earned a Bachelor of Arts in Communication Studies with an emphasis in Journalism. Logan joined our team with extensive experience, having previously written and worked for media entities such as USA Today and Union Broadcasting.

title: Raiders' Biggest Needs Ahead of NFL's Trade Deadline Are Painfully Obvious
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders have looked for ways both big and small during this offseason and the early part of the 2026 regular season.
With the trade deadline approaching, below are the position groups the Raiders should consider trading for.
The Raiders invested heavily in Tyler Linderbaum this offseason. He has already gotten the unit headed in the right direction, but Sunday confirmed that Las Vegas needs additional help along the offensive line. The Raiders started Caleb Rogers over Jackson Powers-Johnson on Sunday.
As expected, Rogers had his ups and downs. Kolton Miller, while still playing well overall, is not quite what he once was. The jury is still out on Spencer Burford. If the Raiders make a trade, finding additional help for their offensive line has to be at the top of that list.
The Raiders are thin at both guard positions. They lack dependable options behind their starting interior offensive linemen. Las Vegas does not know for sure whether the starters they currently have along the interior offensive line are dependable.
Las Vegas kept Cousins clean again on Sunday against the Bills, but still allowed several pressures. They also struggled to run the ball, partly because of issues along their offensive line. Kubiak shared his thoughts on the unit after the Raiders' Week 6 loss to Buffalo.
"I think Spencer has been a really great addition for our team. I think he's a guy that's continuing to improve. Overall, as an offensive line, I really like what we're doing protecting the quarterback,” Kubiak said the day after the game.
“I like how our quarterback's getting the ball out on time, and he knows Spencer and Tyler [Linderbaum] and Kolton [Miller] and DJ [Glaze] and Caleb [Rogers] and the whole offensive line knows that we have to improve in the run game blocking if we want to get to where we want to get.”
If the Raiders were to trade for a player, an offensive lineman would be nice.
The Raiders have a young defensive backfield they trust. Still, Las Vegas' front office and coaching staff knew that the position group was undoubtedly the roster's most vulnerable entering the season.  If they were to make a trade, adding another cornerback would be ideal.
There are few, if any, position groups on Las Vegas' roster that a trade would make more sense for than a trade to boost their defensive backfield moving forward. Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak explained his thoughts on the group.
“I think the best advice you can give them is that you just keep playing. Especially as a defensive back, you're going to get beat, and when you get beat everybody in the free world is going to know it because it's on TV,” Kubiak said.
“When a defensive lineman misses his gap, they're going to show the guy that missed the tackle. So, you got to have thick skin, and you got to move on to the next play. Just keep playing, keep competing,”
Veteran wide receiver Jalen Nailor returned to the Raiders' lineup on Sunday against the Bills. Tre Tucker had a solid overall day that was capped off by an impressive long touchdown pass from Cousins late in the game. Still, the unit leaves much to be desired.
The Raiders still sorely miss Jack Bech, and likely will aim to add another receiver or two next offseason. However, until then, wide receiver will continue to be an issue for Las Vegas unless something changes. If the Raiders were to trade, a receiver may be the top option on their list.
With Nailor back in the fold, Las Vegas' offense seemed to have much more of a chance of moving the ball and scoring points than they did without him in the field in Week 5. Kubiak explained how Nailor impacted the game despite his stats.
"He had targets. He got called on. We threw a double move to him, and they had a penalty on him. He caught a choice route. I thought Jalen [Nailor] was great to have him back. You could feel his presence out there and just got to keep finding ways to get him the ball because he's a really good player. He's a player that I'm counting on, that we're counting on, that's going to continue to ascend," Kubiak said.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Hondo’s Mailbag: Raider Nation Agrees on One Thing
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (3-3) are about to host the Los Angeles Rams (2-4), and while the Silver and Black are overachieving, the preseason unanimous Super Bowl favorite (Rams) is limping into Allegiant Stadium.
With a roster that looks more like an episode of M*A*S*H* than a Super Bowl contender, led by certain Hall of Fame QB Matthew Stafford and a roster full of talent at every position, the Rams are the favorite, but the Raiders have upset on their mind.
While Klint Kubiak has shined this season, GM John Spytek has as well.
The Raiders GM may have painted himself into a corner , according to another NFL executive, but that is not what fans want to talk about.
Each week, I ask Raider Nation on my social media to sound off on their team.  Every week, Raider Nation never fails to deliver, and by the tone and tenor of your comments, the Silver and Black, who see their fandom as a way of life and part of their identity, are all thinking the same thoughts.
Or, as my four-year-old son Dexter Ernest Wayne Carpenter says, “Are you thinking what I am thinking?”
OL giving time and making holes. DL getting pressure on the QB
I am not pretending that Ashton Jeanty has looked like Barry Sanders; he hasn’t, but he also can’t block for himself while toting the rock.
The offensive line will face a stacked box each week until they beat it.  There are many ways to do that, like the play-action pass, but this Tweet nails it.
For the Raiders to upset the Rams, the offensive line will have to have a good day.  Not great, and not even elite, but a good day.
The Rams are primed for an upset here, but the OL has to deliver a much better run-game performance this weekend.
Give Washington the rock 20 times.
I believe the Raiders will not take long to get Mike Washington Jr. more reps this weekend, should Ashton Jeanty struggle early.
I in no way, and neither do the Raiders, place the blame for the lack of a successful running game on Jeanty, but there is no secret that the rookie Arkansas Razorback has delivered some spark.
Kubiak was asked this week about Washington and his role heading into Sunday, and his answer was telling.
"I think we have to get production from all three of our backs, and Mike Washington [Jr.] did some good stuff yesterday, and I thought overall our backs, they ran harder yesterday. I thought they broke tackles. I thought they moved the line of scrimmage when things weren't there. I thought Coach Omar [Young] did a really good job of challenging our guys. I thought they had one of their better games, and I expect that to continue to improve."
No Penalties Finish The Game Score 7 In The Red Zone Not 3 Need A Running Game ☠️🏴‍☠️
This Tweet tells a story that all goes back to the run game.
Penalties kill the running game because you aren’t going to run on third-and-long.  An anemic running game also causes teams to falter in the red zone because of the aforementioned inability to run the ball.
The subsequent lack of a running game turns a seven-point touchdown into a three-point field goal, essentially a loss of four points.
Kirk Cousins said it best after Sunday's loss about the red zone woes: “Anytime you leave points on the board in the red zone, it's hard."

title: Hondo's Raiders Report Card: Roadmap To Ending the Losing Streak
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (3-3) fell short on Sunday in their upset bid against the Buffalo Bills (5-1). The 33-30 loss hurt, but perspective is important.
In their last three games, the Raiders have faced the two favorites to represent the AFC in the Super Bowl: the Kansas City Chiefs and the aforementioned Buffalo Bills.
In both games, the Raiders' upset bids ended not when their opponent beat them, but when they beat themselves.
In the other game, against the reigning AFC representative in the Super Bowl, the New England Patriots , it was a brutal butt-whipping.
That said, the overachieving Raiders continue to move forward with GM John Spytek making roster moves, and Klint Kubiak shining brightly as an NFL first-year coach.
Each Tuesday, throughout the season, I offer you my weekly report card from inside the franchise. An honest assessment, not based on fandom or hatred, no hyperbole, just an honest look at your team. Let’s dig in.
At first glance, a struggling offensive line and no running game may make this seem far-fetched, but let me explain.
The reality is that part of the reason (and no, not the only reason) for the terrible rushing attack is that the opponents know Kubiak’s system. They know his system is built on running the ball, and defenses are selling out to stop it.
It doesn’t mean anemic run game is acceptable; it is not. It needs more attention, but Kubiak discussed his thoughts on the effort on Sunday.
"I think we have to get production from all three of our backs, and Mike Washington [Jr.] did some good stuff yesterday, and I thought overall our backs, they ran harder yesterday. I thought they broke tackles. I thought they moved the line of scrimmage when things weren't there. I thought Coach Omar [Young] did a really good job of challenging our guys. I thought they had one of their better games, and I expect that to continue to improve."
The red zone offense is not good. The Raiders are leaving far too many points on the field with their inability to score in the red zone. Something Kubiak is very aware of.
“Penalties, lack of execution. It's not one thing. But I think mainly when you want to be a good red zone team, you got to run the ball well in the red zone. We didn't do that."
The point is, against a team many feel is on its way to the Super Bowl, the Raiders put up 30 points, and you have the NFL’s leading touchdown-throwing QB, Kirk Cousins.
It isn’t pretty, but the Raiders offense is finding ways to score. It isn’t a beauty contest. Al Davis said, “Just Win, Baby.” He said nothing about pretty. Kubiak agrees.
“The object of the game is to score points, and whether you're getting it done from the ground or from the air, or they're coming from special teams or defensive scores as a team. Obviously, it's a team game, and it's about outscoring the opponent. So, we're never going to – we always want to be great in all facets, okay, but you're going to play to your strengths."
"So, moving the ball and scoring points was good yesterday. However, what do you got to do to get over the hump? You've got to score on all five possessions in the red zone, not just two of five.”
At first, once again, that grade may seem too high. Trust me, it isn’t.
Robbie Leonard, despite a thin DL, a young defensive backfield, and a high-powered offense led by a certain Hall of Fame QB in Josh Allen, did give up 30 points.
But when you look at them holding Allen to one rushing yard, and some of those points coming off offensive mistakes, it was more than impressive; it was outstanding.
Chris Shula, the DC of the Los Angeles Rams, is rightfully discussed as a future head coach in this league, but Leonard just put on a clinic controlling what many consider the best offense in the NFL, and he's had only one bad week this year.
Leonard is an emerging star who can only coach with the roster he's been given, but his head coach trusts him, and they've formed a special tandem.
With John Spytek and his staff building a brilliant roster for the future, the outlook is bright.
Matt Gay, AJ Cole, and long-snapper Alex Ward were great, but still, problems exist.
The Silver and Black special teams unit, for lack of a better term, self-destructed on Sunday through a myriad of costly penalties and, to be kind, poor coverage. They surrendered multiple big returns—including a 40-yard kickoff return to Ray Davis and a 22-yard punt return to Greg Dortch—while committing crucial veteran penalties that repeatedly gave Buffalo prime field position.
I am 100% a supporter of STC Joe DeCamillis, and you should be as well, but this is a rebuilding team, and special teams has been a consistent struggle this season.
DeCamillis will fix it, but it is really ugly.
First-year head coach Klint Kubiak made a rookie mistake when he challenged a play that he shouldn’t have, and that is part of the learning curve. The amazing thing about Kubiak is that, as a first-year coach, he should have had a plethora of mistakes; he hasn’t. You could count his mistakes on one hand and not even need all your fingers.
Robbie Leonard was outstanding, and while Kubiak’s staff has some real stars, this is a rebuilding roster. It is thin, young, and, in many places, void of talent.
Credit the Raiders for not panicking and building the right way.
Without this staff, there's no way the Raiders are 3-3 today, but they are.
This fan base sold a lot of their tickets well before preseason games started. I had several family members and friends who are Bills fans, bought their tickets months ago, and were in town.
That said, I have been to every Raiders game and practice in Allegiant Stadium. The crowd was conservatively 75-25 Bills fans, and I have never seen a crowd that lopsided.
Credit Raider Nation, however: with far more Bills fans in attendance, the crowd was never overwhelming for the Bills, and Raider Nation was loud at all the appropriate times.
As one season ticket holder who sold their tickets told me, “I love what Klint and Spytek are doing; I won’t be selling tickets next year if they keep this up.”
If I had told you back in June that the Raiders would play the Bills as they did, most reasonable people would have laughed.
This loss hurt, because the Raiders beat themselves.
But in the long run, there were a lot of positives you can take from it. If the true direction the leaders of this franchise want to take is a Super Bowl, then Sunday was a yardstick. Reading it, this team may not be as far off as once thought.
The Rams, I suspect, are coming into a buzz saw, a Silver-and-Black buzz saw. If the Raiders play the Rams as they did the Bills and Chiefs, next week we will be talking about an upset.
Can you hear that noise? It’s called optimism, Raider Nation.
Hondo S. Carpenter Sr. is an award-winning sports journalist with decades of experience. He serves as the Senior Writer for NFL and College sports, and is the beat writer covering the Las Vegas Raiders. Additionally, he is the editor and publisher for several sites On SI. Carpenter is a member of the Pro Football Writers Association (PFWA), the Football Writers Association of America (FWAA), and the United States Basketball Writers Association (USBWA).

title: Exclusive: NFL GM Says Raiders’ Spytek 'Painted Him in a Corner'
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (3-3) are overachieving in 2026, a true testimony to what is happening inside the historic franchise.
GM John Spytek has masterfully wielded the helm of the iconic Las Vegas Raiders since the decision was made to move on from Pete Carroll, and hasn’t looked back.
The epic collapse of the franchise in 2025 was no fault of Spytek, but he was charged with cleaning up the mess, and oh, what a job he has done.
I spoke with an NFL GM early today about the Raiders' current situation and my article on four costly free agents who let the team down in their upset bid against the Buffalo Bills last weekend.
Then he pointed out a potential problem looming for the Raiders GM and how he could navigate it.
The GM said, “With WR Jalen Nailor making more money than Superman [Brock Bowers] and WR [Tre Tucker] Tuck, John I am certain is already thinking long and hard about his dilemma.”
I asked him to explain, and he was more than willing to.
“Tuck isn’t a WR1, but he is an excellent WR2. When you are already paying Nailor at a $12 million per year pop, you know his agent isn't going to take that. Not when his guys is producing and the other guy [Nailor] is not.”
I asked him what he thought was the best way to address this.“Carefully.” He laughed. He then went on.
“John has to make sure with Klint he is a key part of the plan moving forward, and I am sure he is. If that is the case, I would move now. With now true lead wide-out, his numbers are only going to go up, and with each good game, not even great, good, his price goes up. Cheaper now, and he can use some of his cap, I know he has some, to eat part of that as a signing bonus on this year. That frees up space in the future.”
He then added a fascinating caveat.
“I have no doubt, and it has only been six games, that they saw this coming, but that deal to Nailor painted him in a corner now. The quicker he moves, if they are sold on him, the smarter it is. But Spy is a smart cookie. Maybe they haven’t seen enough? Want more? Either way, there is path out of the corner, or I can tell you he is smart. Super smart, and this corner could be a blessing in the long run if they get a deal done early, and save cap space from the future.”
I reached out to a prominent agent who is familiar with John Spytek and the WR market. I explained to him the premise of this article and what the NFL GM told me. He added to the comments and assessed Tucker’s value.
“I can’t see any scenario where his agent lets him sign for anything south of $14 million. With a hefty signing bonus, I think a three-year $42 million deal is right in line. Perhaps, if the Raiders really love him, you go four years with a big bonus that could get a smaller number, but not being his agent, I can’t attest to that.”
He added, “If the young man loves the organization and staff, being happy matters over money. I would go for a longer deal, and get it done with the signing bonus. I think John would be thinking three years. Not knowing, either party may say gamble, or specifically the young man on himself or his numbers and he could get more? If he’s happy, I wouldn’t suggest that if the Raiders are in those numbers, let’s do it now.”
In response to the agent's assessment of Tucker's value, I asked the previously mentioned executive. He said, "Nailor is a WR3, and when you look at what true WR2s are getting, at $14 million per deal would be very team-friendly, based on where I think the market is headed, and what his potential numbers will be at the end of the year."
Credit Tucker for how he is playing. For years, the speedster would get open, only to have to wait for a football from a QB who couldn’t hit him in stride. Those days have changed.
On Sunday, QB Kirk Cousins nailed Tre Tucker on a 44-yard touchdown pass. It was a perfect, on-the-money pass that had the Raiders' NFL passing-touchdown-leading QB raving after the game.
Cousins said of Tucker, "I mean, it was a great catch by him on the first one. Great design by our coaches to get him in that position where he's open like that. The second one, he just can roll. I played with DeSean Jackson, I play with Aldrick Robinson, so I played with 4.2 guys; he can roll.”
Cousins wasn’t done with the praise. “And I came off the field, I said, 'I think he's faster than I realize he is.' And there's times where I just need to launch, and he'll go get it. So, he showed me that again today, and big time the way he finished it to go for it and hold on just starts to build trust and respect when a guy goes and makes a play like that."
I asked Kubiak on Monday about Cousins' trust and about using their bond to challenge the defense. He agreed with his QB.
"Yeah, Tre's [Tucker] shown that he can really stress the defense and yeah I agree. Anytime that you can push a ball down the field you know it's going to open things up. So, yeah I agree with you."
I asked Tucker back in August about the simple fact that the Raiders finally have a QB room that can hit him in stride—no waiting around or letting defenders catch up.
His smile and answer told the story then, and his production now backs it up.
"Yeah, it's exciting. I'm just very blessed to be able to play with Kirk [Cousins], Fernando [Mendoza] and Aidan [O’Connell] because those guys just play with anticipation. Like, it's so cool to see. I'll go and watch the quarterback copy of a play, and the quarterback will start on one side and as soon as he flips his hips, the ball's out. It's not like I got to see what he's doing, it's just a trust factor."
"So, that plays a long way. It puts more pressure on us to get open and do our job. But the ball's where it needs to be and that's where a lot of good things happen.”
Hondo S. Carpenter Sr. is an award-winning sports journalist with decades of experience. He serves as the Senior Writer for NFL and College sports, and is the beat writer covering the Las Vegas Raiders. Additionally, he is the editor and publisher for several sites On SI. title: Examining the Mestemaker-to-Miami Draft Opinion Surge
full_text:
There's a lot of time until the 2026 season is over for the Miami Dolphins, but a good chunk of the fan base has already has moved on to next season's NFL Draft, which can shape the future of the franchise depending on who they select.
Any position on the team can receive an upgrade with what will likely be a very high draft pick, if not the first overall. But if the Dolphins were to pull the trigger at quarterback, t hey have a few options to choose from, but one name is standing out as of late.
And, no, it's not Arch Manning, the son of Cooper Manning and nephew to both Peyton and Eli Manning. After a pair of unsuccessful outings for him as of late, the focus has shifted to a redshirt sophomore in the Big 12 Conference.
Drew Mestemaker didn't even begin his football journey as a quarterback. He was a dual-threat option at both punter and safety in high school before making the change to QB when he walked on at North Texas. With the Mean Green, he had one of the best seasons at the position in 2025, recording 4,379 passing yards, 34 touchdowns, and nine interceptions.
When UNT head coach Eric Morris took the job at Oklahoma State ahead of 2026, Mestemaker followed suit, and he hasn't lost a beat despite the tougher competition in the Big 12. Their loss to Tulsa to begin the season has only become more confusing, since they proceeded to take down Oregon the week after, who was ranked ninth in the nation.
The Cowboys then rattled off three more wins before a tough loss on the road to 20th-ranked Houston. Through it all, Mestemaker has had an excellent season with 1,940 yards and 16 touchdowns, but six interceptions through six games, three picks away from his 2025 total, with at least six more games to go.
Regardless, the national consensus has been overwhelmingly positive on Mestemaker and believes he has what it takes to be the first QB picked in the 2027 draft. The following outlets believe the Miami Dolphins will select him with their pick, which is expected to be somewhere in the top three.
CBS (Josh Edwards) - #1 Overall
ESPN (Field Yates) - #2 Overall
SI (Gilbert Manzano) - #2 Overall
Athlon Sports (Luke Easterling) - #3 Overall
Bleacher Report (Brent Sobleski) - #3 Overall
All of these mock drafts have been done within the past seven days, with Ohio State wide receiver Jeremiah Smith ending up on either Tennessee or the Los Angeles Chargers. It's worth noting that the biggest outlet that doesn't think Miami is selecting Mestemaker is USA Today, with Michael Middlehurst-Schwartz predicting the Dolphins will select Smith with the first overall pick.
Mestemaker feels like a jack-of-all-trades quarterback, being able to achieve whatever North Texas and Oklahoma State have asked of him. He has a powerful, accurate arm that coincides with smart decision-making for someone who's only 20 years old. On top of that, he's surprisingly mobile, having rushed for 142 yards and two touchdowns this season.
As mentioned earlier, he has thrown a considerable number of interceptions. It feels like the bad decisions he makes come from trying to do too much, spearheaded by the Cowboys' defense, which gives up 358.2 yards and 23.7 points per game, both on the lower end of the Big 12.
The other big knock on Mestemaker is that there isn't much film to go off of. He didn't play QB at all in high school and has clocked one and a half seasons at the position in college. Granted, what we've been able to witness is a lot of good, but the experience isn't quite there.
With that said, any team that drafts Mestemaker might be better off sitting him for a season, learning from NFL quarterbacks about what to do and what not to do. Look towards Fernando Mendoza, learning from Kirk Cousins and taking the occasional snap during blowouts. Yes, if he's drafted by Miami, that likely means one more season of Malik Willis.
In reality, Mestemaker having a quality season isn't the only reason he's emerged as a top QB in the draft. The other big reason is how Arch Manning has regressed in his senior season. Both he and Texas looked promising, with a 24-23 win over Ohio State, taking the top spot in the nation from the Buckeyes.
After losing to Oklahoma in the Red River Rivalry, then to Florida at home the week after, Texas is currently 19th in the nation. Manning has had a pedestrian season with 1,295 yards, 11 touchdowns, and five interceptions. Granted, he's faced extreme, maybe unfair expectations because of his last name, but this isn't the best time to have a mediocre season with the draft around the corner.
The falloff of Manning has painted a picture of how volatile the position is at college. The outlook on a draft hopeful at any position can drastically change with one bad performance, especially at quarterback. Right now, Mestemaker is the front-runner, but there's no guarantee he'll stay that way after a few weeks, at the end of the regular season, or when a champion is crowned in the CFP.
In the event he isn't, there are a handful of other quarterbacks who could make their case to be a top pick. That includes Miami's Darien Mensah, a Heisman front-runner who's led the top-ranked Hurricanes to an undefeated season up to this point, but he's coming off his worst performance against Florida State. The Canes will hope that this is a one-time occurrence before their premier matchup against Notre Dame on November 7.
Not far behind Mensah is Trinidad Chambliss, who began his college career at Division II Ferris State before leading the Rebels all the way to the Fiesta Bowl last season. Unlike Mestemaker, Chambliss has film for days as a sixth-year senior, but there might be too much, as he's already 24 years old. Only four quarterbacks aged 24 or older have ever been drafted in the first round: Phil Simms, Jim Druckenmiller, Brandon Weeden, and Bo Nix.
One final first-round hopeful (Assuming that Manning continues to struggle) is C.J. Carr. Notre Dame's QB is as smart on the field as he is in the classroom, but he only has 17 starts to his name in college. He'll need a quality performance against a top-rated opponent to become a true top candidate, which could come against the aforementioned Hurricanes in early November.
Jake Gibson is a writer for the Miami Dolphins on SI. He began his sports journalism career with PantherNOW, the student newspaper at his alma mater, Florida International University, where he began as a sportswriter before being promoted to Sports Director. Coming out of college, Jake joined Lemon City Live, where he was able to cover FIU Athletics, the Florida Panthers, NASCAR @ Homestead-Miami Speedway, and the Miami Dolphins, for which he was the beat writer from 2022 to 2024. Jake also works for the Five Reasons Sports Network and is the host of the Shula Bowl Podcast. A native of Homestead, Florida, Jake grew up a South Florida sports fan and has currently attended five Super Bowls in person.

title: Why the Dolphins Should Keep an Eye on Their Former Head Coaches
full_text:
It's starting to look like it could be only a matter of time before former Miami Dolphins head coach Mike McDaniel becomes former Los Angeles Chargers offensive coordinator, and it's a situation the team he led for four seasons (and their fans) should monitor.
McDaniel's offense turned in yet another poor performance during a Week 6 loss at Kansas City that dropped the Chargers to 0-6 on the season, leaving them as one of only two teams this season without a win.
The other, of course, is the Dolphins, who will take an 0-5 record into MetLife Stadium coming off their bye next Sunday.
The Chargers scored a season-low six points against the Chiefs on Sunday, the fifth time in six games they failed to score more than 17 and it doesn't take long watching them to see how disjointed and dysfunctional the whole offensive operation looks, from a badly regressing Justin Herbert at quarterback to an offensive line that's again among the worst in the NFL and dealing again with injuries to their quality starting tackles, Rashawn Slater and Joe Alt.
Things haven't improved one bit since a shocking loss against Arizona in the opener and it might be that Jim Harbaugh will have no choice but to fire McDaniel to, if nothing else, inject some life into an offense that has shown little while the defense keeps battling.
Harbaugh's comments after the loss at Kansas City and heading into the Chargers' bye didn't sound great for McDaniel when he said he would have to evaluate things when asked whether McDaniel would continue calling plays.
And, of course, where it gets fun for Dolphins fans is that the logical replacement for McDaniel based on play-calling experience is the man who preceded McDaniel's predecessor, Adam Gase.
Gase had been out of the NFL since he was fired by the New York Jets after the 2020 season when the Chargers hired him as a pass game specialist, and the question is what kind of changes he might make to the offensive scheme if he were to take over.
This is important because McDaniel's complex scheme clearly isn't a fit with Herbert and the rest of the offense with its complicated verbiage, shifts and motions, and timing-based offense. That scheme worked for a while in Miami, and it's fair to ask how much of that was the presence and skill set of Tua Tagovailoa at quarterback and how much was prime Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle overwhelming defenses with their speed.
The reality is that if the Chargers don't make a change, it's difficult to envision them winning many games navigating a schedule that's about as tough as that of the Dolphins.
It does seem at the moment as though a major revamping is needed for the Chargers to have offensive success and win some games.
As it stands Monday morning, the Chargers hold the first position in the 2027 draft order and it could be that it comes down to them or the Dolphins for that No. 1 spot.
And it very well might be that the status quo would benefit the Dolphins in this instance, and that status quo is the Chargers keeping McDaniel.
Meanwhile, McDaniel's three coordinators from last season all are enjoying some team success this season.
Former offensive coordinator Frank Smith now is an assistant head coach with the Minnesota Vikings, who at 5-0 stand as one of the three undefeated teams in the NFL — though it should be pointed out that team's success has a lot more to do with the defense coordinator by Brian Flores.
Former defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver is handling the same role with the Baltimore Ravens, who are in a three-way tie atop the AFC North, although the team just squandered a 13-3 fourth-quarter lead in a last-second loss against divisional foe Cleveland on Sunday.
Lastly, special teams coordinator Danny Crossman now works for the team tied for first at 4-2 in the AFC North, the Pittsburgh Steelers.

title: 10 Stats That Help Explain the Dolphins' Tough Start (And What Can Be Done About Them)
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins sat out the Week 6 action of the 2026 NFL regular season before getting back to work Monday looking to bounce back after an 0-5 start.
While stats often can be deceiving stats, we've come up with 10 numbers that help explain the winless start along with some analysis as to how to move those numbers in the right direction.
29.5 — That's the gap in completion percentage for Malik Willis from his 2025 season with the Green Bay Packers (85.7) and his first five games with the Dolphins (56.2)
Nobody should expect a full-time quarterback to come close to an 85 percent completion rate, but 56 percent isn't good enough and Willis can help himself by simply being willing to accept and take the safe, short completions.
10.1 — That's Willis intended air yards per pass attempt, according to Pro Football Reference. That figure leads the NFL, with Lamar Jackson second at 9.8.
This goes right to our first point. The Dolphins maybe need to stop taking shots down the field with a less-than-stellar wide receiver group.
3.2 — That's the average yards of separation for Malik Washington, which is the highest figure of any Dolphins player. That figure is tied for 35th-best in the NFL. The next-best Dolphins player in that category is tight end Greg Dulcich at 2.6, all the way down to tied for 79th in the NFL.
And this number illustrates, only in part, the issues with the wide receiver group.
3:09 — That's the Dolphins' rushing average on first-and-10 rushing attempts, tied with the Philadelphia Eagles for second-worst in the NFL, with only the Green Bay Packers doing worse.
Ollie Gordon II is coming off two productive games in relief of De'Von Achane, so maybe this number will improve organically after the bye without having to make any kind of schematic adjustments.
3:09 — That's Ollie Gordon II's NextGen Stats efficiency number, which measures the yards ran per yard gained, with the lower the number the most North-South the runner is. Gordon's figure is second-best in the NFL behind only the 3.01 of the Chicago Bears' Kyle Monangai.
This is what we're talking about with Gordon ... maybe the Dolphins need to give him more first-down carries.
76.0 — That's the completion percentage allowed by the Dolphins, which is on track to set a dubious NFL record. The record currently belongs to the 2016 Detroit Lions at 72.7 percent, according to StatMuse.
We get that part of Jeff Hafley's defensive scheme involves a willingness to give up short completions, but at some point the coverage needs to tighten up, particularly if the pass rush doesn't start getting to the quarterback.
4 — That's the number of sacks for the Dolphins through five games, their lowest total at this stage since at least 1981. They had five sacks in the first five games of 2019.
And that brings us to this, though it's never all about sack numbers but also affecting the quarterback. And the Dolphins have come up short on both ends. This might require more blitzing, which will leave the secondary more vulnerable to big plays, but getting nickel-and-dimed to death as they were against Cincinnati last week might not be much better.
41.27 — That's the Dolphins offense's third-down conversion rate, 12th-best in the NFL through Week 5. The only time since 2010 the Dolphins have finished a season with a higher conversion rate was in 2023 (the 11-6 season) when they were at 42.08.
Imagine how much better it could be if the Dolphins did better with their first-and-10 rushes. This also is one positive for Willis in the midst of all the criticism (some of it warranted) thrown in his direction.
34.1 — That's the kickoff return average allowed by the Dolphins, which puts Miami dead last in the NFL. It's on pace for the Dolphins' worst showing since 2023 when they finished 32nd by allowing 30.5 yards per kickoff return.
The Dolphins have used 53 different players on special teams, and the only way this gets better is continuing to churn the roster to find answers because we're thinking (at this point) it's not a schematic issue.
0 — That's the number of leads the Dolphins have held this season, one short of the NFL record of six games to start a season without a lead, a mark that belongs to the 2005 Houston Texans.
And we close with maybe the most painful stat of all, and will repeat our suggestion from last week that the Dolphins should elect to receive if they win the coin toss. Yes, it's usually preferable to defer to be able to potentially get the back-to-back possessions, but desperate times call for desperate measures. And there are times when playing with a lead or a deficit changes game strategy. And it would be nice for the Dolphins not to be chasing the game all the time, like they did against Cincinnati when they won the toss, deferred, gave up an 81-yard kickoff return and were down 7-0 before a minute of game action had expired.

title: Where to Assign Blame For the Dolphins' Grounded Passing Attack
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins passing game has been abysmal. Through five weeks, they’re tied for last in terms of EPA per pass, and Malik Willis has the lowest completion rate in the NFL among qualified quarterbacks.
There’s more than enough blame to go around for this fluttering offense, with multiple groups and individuals needing to improve.
Miami’s offensive coordinator, Bobby Slowik, is running very similar concepts to those from the previous regime, which makes sense considering Slowik was the senior passing game coordinator under Mike McDaniel.
That isn’t a pass, however, for a scheme that, to this point, hasn’t matched the skill sets of its players or the philosophy on defense.
Jeff Hafley’s defensive system has been ultra-conservative, playing with deep safeties and linebackers to limit explosives and slow down the pace of the game. Rather than matching this with a ball-control style of offense, however, Slowik has thrown haymakers more than about every other offense in football. Through week five, Miami’s offense ranks fourth in pass attempts of 20+ yards, but is fourth-worst in terms of EPA per dropback on those looks, per NextGenStats.
Miami’s pass plays look far too similar to what they ran for Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle, especially considering this receiving corps is among the youngest in football and is bereft of top-end talent. Their two-man concepts are non-threatening when being run by rookies Chris Bell and Kevin Coleman Jr., especially when paired with a first down rushing attack that ranks second-to-last in success rate, meaning defenses don’t bite down as hard on play action.
Miami hasn’t put together an honest effort to get Malik Willis easy completions on early downs, instead playing touchdown-to-checkdown for a quarterback who hasn’t been willing to take the latter. Instead, Slowik has pressed early, Miami has fallen behind the sticks, and he has placed Willis in disadvantageous situations for large portions of each game.
A lack of top-end talent is one thing, but as former Dolphins head coach Brian Flores once harkened on, many of this group’s mistakes take no talent to fix.
Inexperience has shown up early and often for the receiver group. On crucial downs, receivers line up in the wrong spot, with the primary culprit being third-round rookie Chris Bell, who notably missed a vast majority of the offseason while recovering from an ACL tear. Malik Willis is forced to redirect traffic late in the play clock, rather than having the time to survey the defense pre-snap.
There have also been gaffes in route-running that have made life difficult on the young quarterback. On Willis’ first pass against Cincinnati, a deep shot to Malik Washington, both Washington and coach Jeff Hafley said the receiver turned the wrong direction, pushing the route to the sideline, rather than vertically up the numbers.
Later in that same game, three of Miami’s eligibles, lined up in a bunch, comically bumped into each other, throwing off the timing of a route concept.
The Miami Dolphins passing game is BROKEN. Sure, Malik Willis bears some of the blame, but there have been countless errors out of his control that have contributed to poor results. pic.twitter.com/xDFvnHPT8U
Their scramble drill procedures have been off as well. The spacing has become congested late in plays, and it’s clear players aren’t sure where to go. On Willis’ second interception of Week 5, Malik Washington stayed in one spot, bringing his defender into the window where Willis attempted to throw the ball to Kevin Coleman Jr.
Miami’s top four receivers (including the injured Caleb Douglas) are all in their third year or younger, and they need to grow up fast if they want to make the plays needed to start winning games.
Miami’s new quarterback bears plenty of blame for Miami’s failed aerial assault. It’s unfair to ask him to put out all of the fires started by his supporting cast, but he will be judged on whether or not he gets burned.
On the aforementioned interception intended for Kevin Coleman Jr., for instance, Willis can’t control whether Washington operates the scramble drill correctly. However, he had more than enough time to see that Coleman was running into defenders and live to play another down.
Despite the sixth-best time-to-pressure in the NFL, Willis ranks 23rd in pressure-to-sack rate, per PFF. As the film has shown, these sacks often happen in back-breaking situations, such as second down inside the 5-yard line in Week 5, where he had plenty of time to throw the ball away, but made an abysmal decision to hold on to it.
Quicker decision-making will be the biggest key for Willis. His process has yet to speed up the requisite level to avoid major mistakes. He needs to be able to consistently get through his progressions, while also deciphering when to abandon the pocket or give up on a play. Thus far, he looks like a quarterback who has only started eleven career games, when this version of the Dolphins needs a higher level of maturation in order to put together complete performances.
Tyler DeSena is currently a journalism student at the University of Central Florida. Prior to joining Dolphins On SI in 2026, DeSena worked with dolphinstalk.com, and created independent social media content on X, YouTube and TikTok.

title: Quick Thought on Each Dolphins Defensive Starter
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins are into their bye weekend after a disappointing 0-5 start made worse by the fact they have yet to hold a lead, which is a good time to examine what has stood out about all the players who have started at least one game.
There have been 16 of those on defense, so here's a thought on each from Zach Sieler to Julius Wood.
DT ZACH SIELER — Sieler remains a very solid starter at a minimum and he would be a long-term fixture on this team under different circumstances. But he could wind up moved out at some point during this rebuilding project.
DT JORDAN PHILLIPS — Because of the role he plays, Phillips never will be a star, but he's a valuable member of the defense when it comes to stopping the run.
DT ZEEK BIGGERS — There's potential with Biggers, particularly as a big lineman who can move around on the defensive line, but there also hasn't been nearly enough impact just yet.
EDGE CHOP ROBINSON — Some of the analytics suggest Robinson is being very effective as a pass rusher, but the film suggests otherwise (other than the Minnesota game). That said, he still does look better than last season; it's just that the Dolphins need more from him.
EDGE JOSHUA UCHE — There haven't been flashy plays, but it says here that it's Uche who's been the best edge defender for the Dolphins, to the point where maybe the team needs to consider bringing back him next season.
EDGE ROBERT BEAL JR. — There was very little noticeable about Beal in the first two games before he landed on injured reserve, so the hope is he flashes when he comes back from his hamstring injury.
LB JORDYN BROOKS — Brooks hasn't been the dominating force he was in 2025 (especially in the second half of the season), but there obviously are tough circumstances at play, including a training camp injury. That said, while he's been overshadowed by Jacob Rodriguez, he's actually graded out better so far if you go by the Pro Football Focus numbers.
LB JACOB RODRIGUEZ — It's been quite the start for Rodriguez, who has demonstrated the great instincts he showed at Texas Tech, and though we feel at times his performance has been oversold, he's certainly got the look of a long-term fixture at linebacker at worst and a future All-Pro at best.
LB WILLIE GAY JR. — Gay still looks like the most athletic linebacker on the team, but he also looks like he'll get caught out of position from time to time.
CB CHRIS JOHNSON — Johnson has rebounded nicely from a rough start that includes a forgettable Week 1 outing against the Raiders and he's impressed from the start with his tackling ability.
CB JASON MARSHALL JR. — Because the Dolphins have played a lot of soft zones, the defense hasn't gotten beat over the top but there also have been very few pass breakups. All that said, Marshall has been solid and looks like a keeper.
CB JUJU BRENTS — It's the same old story with Brents, who still totally looks the part of an elite cornerback and plays that way at times. But then there's always the feeling it's a matter of time before he gets injured. The Cincinnati game was a great example because he was outstanding before leaving the game not once but twice.
S MICHAEL TAAFFE — Props to Taaffe for earning a starting job as a rookie fifth-round pick and that was thanks in large part to his off-the-chart intangibles. The question with Taaffe continues to concern his NFL ceiling because of his lack of ideal size and athleticis.
S DANTE TRADER JR. — Still not quite sure why Trader wasn't in the starting lineup from the start of the regular season, but he's back in there now and his physical presence is quite welcome in the back end.
S ZAYNE ANDERSON — A special teams specialist in Green Bay, Anderson got his shot as the opening-day starter, but it went south pretty quickly for him and now he's back to mostly being a special-teamer.
S JULIUS WOOD — Wood got one start when he was the nickel against the Kansas City Chiefs to open the game with Johnson and Marshall outside, but he's played 17 snaps on defense the whole year. His role is on special teams.

title: How the Waddle Trade Keeps Looking Better and Better for the Dolphins
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins sacrificed the present for a better future when they moved Jaylen Waddle in the offseason, but their big trade with the Denver Broncos continues to look good in the moment.
While Waddle had yet another uneventful outing in the Broncos' ugly Thursday night overtime victory against the Seattle Seahawks on Thursday night, the main piece the Dolphins in the trade got some national love Friday morning.
In short, a trade we liked very much from the start has become one we downright love at this point.
To refresh everyone's memory, the Dolphins traded Waddle and a 2026 fourth-round pick (111th overall) to Denver for the 30th overall pick, and picks in the third (94th overall) and fourth rounds (130th overall).
The Dolphins then moved the 30th overall along with the 90th overall selection to the San Francisco 49ers for the 27th overall selection and the 138th overall pick in the fourth round.
With the 27th pick, the Dolphins selected cornerback Chris Johnson, then took wide receiver Chris Bell with the 94th pick, linebacker Trey Moore with the 130th pick and safety Kyle Louis with the 138th pick.
So looking at the complete deal, it comes down to the Dolphins trading Waddle, the 90th pick and the 111th pick for Chris Johnson, Chris Bell, Trey Moore and Kyle Louis.
Oh, and the Dolphins cleared Waddle from their books moving forward, though they did take a $23 million dead cap hit for him in 2026.
It probably will take a couple of years before a final verdict can be rendered on this trade, but the early indications are that it was a big win for Miami.
Regardless of what happened, it helped accomplished the goal of clearing the books beyond this one year of pain, but Waddle's production in Denver through the first six games has eliminated any buyer's remorse.
In Denver's 17-14 victory against Seattle, Waddle had four catches for only 24 yards, the fifth time in six games he failed to top 35 receiving yards.
Since his one big game, a 138-yard performance in Week 2 against Jacksonville, Waddle has recorded 13 catches for 88 yards in the past four games combined.
That four-game stretch is the worst of his career in terms of yardage, not even remotely close to his previous four-game low of 135 yards during the 2024 season.
Waddle was expected to provide the big-play element to a Denver team that reached the AFC Championship Game last year, but instead their offense has faced little but criticism this season even though the team still has a 4-2 record.
Meanwhile in Miami, we also could make the argument that Johnson has performed better, particularly considering he's a rookie.
While the start of his NFL career was bumpy, he has been impressive of late, enough that Sports Illustrated draft analyst Justin Melo mentioned him among his five rookies on the move.
Bell is off to a slow start in his first NFL season, but that's somewhat to be expected considering he's coming back from a serious knee injury and the Dolphins offense as a whole has been dysfunctional.
Moore and Louis are on injured reserve and it's safe to wonder how much they will contribute, if at all, in 2026.
But Moore looked like he was ready in camp to become a major contributor, and Louis will be given a chance at a new position when he returns.
Either way, this trade is looking very good indeed at this time.

title: The Five Dolphins Players Who Must Step Up After the Bye
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins were expected to have a tough time in 2026 given all their roster changes and more importantly their lack of financial resources with so much money committed to players no longer around.
But the expectation also was that there would be gradual improvement and hopefully some measure of success at some point.
At 0-5 heading into their bye weekend without once having a lead, the Dolphins obviously have failed in the success department.
If that's going to change once the Dolphins return to action, starting in Week 7 against the New York Jets at MetLife Stadium, they're going to need for some players to start delivering on their promise and raise their level of play.
We'll start with the obvious one because as the quarterback he's the player with the most influence on the final result.
It would be great if Willis got better performances from the people around him and the mistakes and missed assignments would go away, but Willis also has to do his part.
Through the first five games, Willis has shown flashes of brilliance here and there, but there haven't been enough of those while there have been too many missed opportunities. The hope is that Week 5 performance against Cincinnati will end up being the low point for his season and it's all upward from now.
This isn't about Douglas having not performed, he just wasn't around the past three games and it's pretty obvious that maybe he could have made a difference.
In the opener against the Las Vegas Raiders, Douglas showed what kind of factor he could be for Willis and the passing game, and there's just no way to overstate how feeble the passing game has looked since he's been out.
If we are to believe certain analytics like pass rush win rate, Robinson has done just fine so far this season when he's been in the lineup, but the film shows a different reality.
For example, Pro Football Focus gave Robinson a total of four pressures in the Week 5 loss against the Cincinnati Bengals with two hits and two hurries, but the reality is he didn't really affect Joe Burrow because those hits and hurries came after the ball had been released. One example was the touchdown pass to Samaje Perine in the second quarter where Robinson did get to Burrow but from the side and after the ball was released, therefore not affecting the play.
That's what the Dolphins need from Robinson.
It's not about sacks or forced fumbles, but rather affecting the quarterback. One example of that was Willis' first interception where his arm was hit as he threw the ball. That's a real QB pressure and QB hit.
Yes, Robinson has looked better — particularly against Minnesota — this season than he has before, but that should not be the bar for him. The bar for him should be to become an impact player.
Maybe that happens after the bye.
Another one, as with Willis, that seems pretty obvious.
Here, though, there are two reasons it would be very beneficial if Jackson could raise his level of play: The first is it obviously would benefit the offense and Willis; the second is it would help his market value if the Dolphins indeed decide to move him before the NFL trade deadline.
Jackson's work in the run game has been solid, but he really needs to pick it up when it comes to pass protection.
If he doesn't, the Dolphins at some point should and/or will consider removing him from the lineup.
Yes, there are a few other players on offense or defense we could have mentioned here, particularly if we're looking at the big picture, but we're focusing now on winning a game or two.
And the Dolphins aren't good enough right now where they can afford the kind of miscues we've seen from Riley Patterson, whether it's a missed field goal, missed extra point or a kickoff that falls short of the landing zone and gives the opponent the ball at the 40-yard line (he got bailed out against Cincinnati on that last one because of a roughness penalty on the Bengals).

title: Three Reasons for Optimism at the Bye for the Dolphins
full_text:
If you look hard enough, you can find positives from the Miami Dolphins amid their bye week, even if their winless record is enough to write off their season completely.
The Dolphins have fought through adversity, including critical injuries and some of the NFL's best opponents, just to get to their bye week. It might be lost on some how young and inexperienced this roster and coaching staff are, but they've still battled against top-tier talent like Kansas City, Minnesota, and Cincinnati.
Now, they get a week off to rest and recover before a trip to New York to take on the Jets. Miami is still searching for its first win, but a few positives could help them get the job done sooner rather than later.
Anyone who had doubts that Aaron Brewer was not worth the three-year, $52.5 million contract extension is running out of reasons to doubt. All in all, Brewer has been near-flawless to start this season and should be considered one of the best centers in football.
Having clocked 292 snaps, he's been responsible for zero sacks against Malik Willis and has  committed only three penalties. Pro Football Focus has given Brewer an overall grade of 68.2 - the eighth-best out of 34 qualified centers.
What makes Brewer truly stand out is his ability to run block, being a key creator of space for Ollie Gordon II and Miami's ensemble of running backs. His PFF run grade is a 76 flat - the third-best in the NFL. His most impressive performance came against Minnesota - no QB hits, sacks, or penalties, and only one pressure on 39 snaps.
Even more surprising than Brewer, however, has been the resurgence of Jonah Savaiinaea. Many fans were ready to give up on him following a disastrous 2025 season, but switching him back to right guard has helped him grow exponentially.
Clean is the name of the game for Savaiinaea - he's committed no penalties and is responsible for no sacks so far this season on 244 snaps. His performance against San Francisco was as close to perfect as you can get - zero pressures and hurries on 59 snaps.
That said, Savaiinaea suffered an ankle injury in Miami's loss to Cincinnati, and the week off might be just what he needs to recover, but even MORE surprisingly, his replacement was just as effective. Jarrett Kingston came in and held his own, including a noteworthy pancake block on Dexter Lawrence II on his second snap.
There are some fans who might not agree with the decision to draft Kadyn Proctor in the first round, but Proctor has done nothing but justify his selection. It hasn't always been perfect, but you can't deny that only three penalties and one sack through 292 snaps isn't fantastic for a rookie playing left guard for the first time since his freshman season at Alabama.
The major rookie sensation, however, has been linebacker Jacob Rodriguez. Through Week Five, he leads the NFL in tackles (57). He's also recorded three tackles for a loss, a pass deflection, and is one of 25 linebackers with an interception. These are first-round numbers being done by someone who was picked 43rd overall, and justify consideration for the Defensive Rookie Of The Year Award.
Chris Johnson might have had a shaky start to the season, but he's ramped up his play since Week Three. When playing in man coverage, he's allowed seven receptions (sixth least in the NFL), 29 receiving yards (third least), and 4.1 yards per catch (second least).
Caleb Douglas was looking like the answer the Dolphins needed at wide receiver following a stellar performance against Las Vegas in Week One, racking up 94 yards on five receptions. Unfortunately, an ankle injury he suffered the following week has sidelined him up to this point, and for Miami's sake, they'll want him back as soon as possible.
Douglas, alongside Chris Bell and Michael Taaffe, has been part of a rookie core that has shown potential for years to come, and the Dolphins still have Kyle Louis and Trey Moore in the stash. All in all, general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan did a solid job finding rookie talent in his first season for the Dolphins, which is raising expectations for Miami in a possible make-or-break 2027 Draft.
It would have been easy to write off Miami's running game following De'Von Achane's ACL injury that he suffered against Kansas City. It admittedly looked shaky the rest of the way against the Chiefs, but they got things under control not long after.
The credit goes to the aforementioned offensive line alongside Ollie Gordon II, who has turned into a reliable starter for the Dolphins with 236 rushing yards and three touchdowns, leading the team in both categories. Since becoming Miami's starter, he's averaged 5 rushing yards per attempt, which is the eighth-most in the NFL.
He's been a drive extender, responsible for nine first downs and seven explosive runs, which are runs that net 10 yards or more. He had a brief scare in the Cincinnati game, going to the blue medical tent midway through the game, but returned not long after.
It hasn't all been perfect, however. Jaylen Wright hasn't been an effective backup, with Willis having to do more with his legs to partially compensate. We'll see if the Dolphins continue to stick with Wright as the second option in the backfield or look somewhere else - they missed their opportunity with Jerome Ford, who had a tryout for Miami but ended up signing with Arizona's practice squad.
At the end of the day, the Dolphins average 126.6 rushing yards per game, the 11th-most in the NFL. It could have been much worse considering the loss of Achane, but Gordon has done more than enough to carry the offense on his back at times.

title: The Best, Worst and Most Likely Outcomes for Vikings vs. Colts
full_text:
The Vikings are getting healthy after their bye week , and the first test after a week away will be against the spiraling Indianapolis Colts. Still, despite the Vikings being favorites, anything can happen in this league, like, say a 33-0 comeback.
Ideally, the Vikings move to 6-0 with a demonstrative win, but it may not be so simple. Here are the best, worst and likliest scenarios for Minnesota's matchup with the Colts in Week 7.
The bye week came at a fortunate time for getting players healthy, but it also might have taken a bit of wind out of the sails of the 5-0 Vikings.
Murray played his best game of the season against the Saints, but will now need to regain a bit of steam against Indianapolis after getting the week off. Fortunately, the 2-4 Colts are fresh off a loss to what were the winless Titans, and will likely be without their top defender in Sauce Gardner. With a healthy receiving corps and the return of Jordan Mason, the excuses will be few and far between for Murray on Sunday.
And while there's little question that the defense will once again show up for Minnesota, they do need keep the injury bug away . Eight defensive starters have played at least 80% of the snaps this season, and their health has been key to driving one of the best defenses in football. Coming out of Week 7 without injury will be the ultimate goal in what should otherwise be a quick dispatch of Daniel Jones and company.
Five games into the season, opposing offenses still haven't figured out how to break Flores' scheme, but at some point there's bound to be some progress. Obviously teams know the pressure is coming, but the difficult part of playing the Vikings is their disguises and pre-snap confusion. Still, no system is without their tells, and eventually you'd think some team latches on to something...anything.
A loss to Indy isn't the end of the world, but if Shane Steichen exposes a crack in the armor, the Vikings defense may be forced to get even more creative the rest of the way (if such a thing is possible).
On offense, things are trending up, but Minnesota is still looking for much better production out of Jordan Addison and Jauan Jennings. If neither impress against the Colts, the trade talks for either may see a big spike.
Jennings' name has already been a hot topic after notching just two catches on the season, but Addison may fetch more value, and is already on track for a third-straight year of worse production than his standout rookie year.
The combined record from the Vikings previous three opponents is just 3-14, which isn't exactly a ringing endorsement of their undefeated season. The Colts are 2-4, and just lost to the previously 0-5 Titans, prompting the firing of longtime general manager Chris Ballard. A win is expected here to move to 6-0, but it won't do much to dispel the notions that Minnesota is punching above their weight this season.
National opinions aside, though, the Vikings offense hopefully once again shows some progress, while the defense continues their historic level of dominance. At this point, the playoffs are almost a certainty with a 91% chance according to ESPN, so marginal improvement week-to-week is the most important thing.

title: Another Potential Demond Claiborne Replacement Just Became Available for Vikings
full_text:
The Minnesota Vikings are 5-0 heading into Week 7 and sitting at the top of the NFC North. While that is great for now, there are areas of the roster that could be improved to prepare for the remainder of the games on the schedule.
One position where the Vikings could use a boost is running back. While Jordan Mason was out, Aaron Jones Sr. was responsible for getting production on the ground since Demond Claiborne and DeeJay Dallas have struggled to be effective.
Mason is on track to return against the Indianapolis Colts on Sunday, but Minnesota could still use depth beyond their one-two punch of Jones and Mason. A recently released running back could help to improve that situation.
On Tuesday, the Philadelphia Eagles announced that they waived running back Jaydon Blue. Blue was picked up by the Eagles at the start of September, but didn't see any game action.
The 22-year-old rusher joined the Dallas Cowboys as a fifth-round pick in the 2025 NFL Draft and played five games as a rookie.
Blue ended his rookie campaign with 38 rushing attempts for 129 yards and a touchdown. He picked up seven first downs for Dallas and averaged 3.4 yards per carry. The Cowboys waived him as part of their final roster cuts, which led him to the Eagles' practice squad.
The Vikings are currently ranked 22nd in rushing yards per attempt at 3.8. However, Claiborne has struggled mightily as a rookie, averaging only 2.2 yards per rushing attempt on six carries this season, making him an unreliable third option for Minnesota.
Claiborne is only 23 years old, so there's plenty of time for him to find his footing in the NFL. But until he can, the Vikings might want to look into a player like the 5-foot-9, 198-pound Blue to hold down the RB3 job until he is ready.
During the 2025 NFL Scouting Combine, Blue ran an impressive 4.38 seconds in the 40-yard dash, which is a great measure of his speed. The only question marks surrounding him at this point in his career are his maturity and fashion sense.
Last year, Blue wore a pair of Louis Vuitton-Nike cleats at practice, and it did not go over well. The footwear gave him blisters. His footwear choice gave him a reputation for choosing style over function, which did not go over well with the team or fans.
Nonetheless, if a tryout and physical go well for the young running back, the Vikings might be smart to add him to the practice squad and potentially elevate him to the 53-man roster if they need a speedy running back with some experience to take pressure off Jones or Mason.

title: Harrison Smith Is Slowly Becoming a Concern for Vikings (Even If It Hurts to Say)
full_text:
If you go to a Minnesota Vikings game at U.S. Bank Stadium, you will probably see quite a few fans wearing a #22 Harrison Smith jersey. Now in his 15th season with the Purple and Gold, the veteran safety is universally loved and respected for his contributions to the team.
It was exciting when it was announced that Smith would return for the 2026 NFL season . A future Vikings Ring of Honor player, giving fans one more season of his hard-hitting, smothering play.
However, that is not what fans are getting this season. Instead, the six-time Pro Bowl, one-time All-Pro First-Team, and one-time All-Pro Second-Team defender has seldom been on the field. And when he is on the field, he looks like a shell of his former self.
This season, Smith is playing less than half of the Vikings' defensive snaps. Of a possible 295 plays, he has been in on 140. He hasn't started a single one of Minnesota's first five games.
Smith's limited role in defensive coordinator Brian Flores' scheme isn't a problem, but there is an issue with his effectiveness on the field. His Pro Football Focus grade of 31.5 says it all. Smith is ranked dead last among 98 qualifying safeties.
The 37-year-old defensive back has been particularly bad in pass coverage. His PFF grade of 33.5 is the second-worst of all qualifying safeties this year. He has recorded seven combined tackles, three pass defenses, and a quarterback hit in the team's first five games.
What makes the situation even more complicated is that the player benefiting from extra playing time by picking up Smith's reps this year is Josh Metellus. In fact, Metellus has played all 295 defensive snaps for Minnesota so far this season.
The problem is that Metellus is struggling almost as badly as Smith. His 40.2 PFF grade ranks him 93rd among 98 safeties, and his 33.4 pass coverage grade, while allowing a 145.8 passer rating, is unacceptable.
The Vikings have done a good job hiding Smith and Metellus' struggles this year, but there will be a time when the team won't be able to pick up the slack, and an opposing offense will exploit their safety weakness.
It hurts to say it, but the Vikings need to figure out a way to get better play from Smith if they want to be contenders this year.
